I forgot to write you about it earlier, and only remembered when you asked me. As I’m sure you know, chocolate disappears instantly at the boardinghouse, you hardly realize you’ve been given chocolates and they’re gone. But regarding Josef, there’s something else I wanted to tell you: As I mentioned, I couldn’t get in to see him because he was busy with a gentleman. After I’d waited patiently for a while, I asked an assistant whether the appointment would last much longer. I asked what sort of a trial it was, whether he might be mistaken, but he said it was no mistake, it was a trial and a serious one at that, but that’s all he knew. translation: As soon as the greeting – not that he had time to sit down in the armchair, which his uncle invited him to – was over, he asked K. for a short conversation in private. "It is necessary," he said, swallowing with difficulty, "it is necessary for my peace of mind." K. immediately sent the servant out of the room, instructing him not to admit anyone. "What have I heard, Josef?" his uncle called out when they were alone, sitting on the table and shoving various papers underneath him without looking, so that he could sit more comfortably. K. remained silent; he knew what was to come, but suddenly, relieved from the exhausting work, as he was, he gave in to a pleasant fatigue and gazed out the window at the opposite side of the street, of which only a small, triangular piece was visible from his seat, a section of empty wall between two shopfronts. "You're gazing out the window!" his uncle exclaimed, raising his arms. "For goodness' sake, Josef, answer me, is it true, can it possibly be true?" "Dear uncle," said K., and shook himself out of his distraction, "I don't know what you're asking me." "Josef," said the uncle warningly, "you've always told the truth, as far as I know. Should I take your last words as an ominous sign?" "I sense what you want," said K. obediently, "you've probably heard about my trial." "So it is," replied the uncle, nodding slowly, "I've heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote to me," said the uncle, "she hasn't had any contact with you, you don't take much care of her, but she learned about it. I received the letter today and, of course, I came straight away. Not for any other reason, but it seems like a sufficient reason. I can read you the relevant passage." He pulled out the letter from his wallet. "Here it is." It reads: "Dear Uncle, I haven't seen Josef for a long time, last week I went to the bank, but Josef was too busy to see me; I had to wait for nearly an hour, then I had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak with him, perhaps we'll have the opportunity again soon. On his name day, he sent me a large box of chocolates, it was very nice and considerate of him. I forgot to write to you about it, I only remembered it now, when you asked me. Chocolates, you know, disappear in the boarding house as soon as one becomes aware that one has been gifted with them; they're gone in no time. But as for Josef, I wanted to tell you something. As mentioned, I wasn't admitted to him at the bank because he was in negotiations with a gentleman. After waiting for a while in silence, I asked a servant if the negotiations would take long. He said they probably would, since it was likely that they were dealing with the trial against the Prokurist. I asked him what kind of trial it was, if he wasn't mistaken, he replied that he wasn't mistaken, that it was a trial, and a serious one, but he knew no more. He himself would have liked to help the Prokurist, as he was a good and just man, but he didn't know how to start and only wished that influential people would take it upon themselves to intervene. This would certainly happen, and it would probably have a good outcome in the end, but for now, as he gathered from the Prokurist's mood, it was not going well. I didn't attach much importance to this, I also tried to calm down the silly servant, forbade him from speaking about it to others, and considered it just gossip. Still, it might be a good idea if, on your next visit, you looked into the matter further, it would be easy for you to get more information, and if it really needs to be done, you could use your influential connections to intervene. But if it's not necessary, which is the most likely scenario, then Erna will soon have the opportunity to give you a hug, which would please her." – "A good child," said the uncle, after finishing the reading, and wiped away some tears from his eyes. K. nodded, he had completely forgotten about Erna, even her birthday, and the story about the chocolates was probably made up just to protect him from the uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and with the theatre tickets he intended to send her regularly from now on, he wouldn't be able to reward her enough, but he didn't feel suited for visits to the boarding house and for conversations with an 18-year-old high school student. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who had forgotten all about the urgency and agitation caused by the letter and was reading it again. "Yes, uncle," said K., "it's true." "True?" exclaimed the uncle.
source_text: Gleich nach der Begrüßung – sich in den Fauteuil zu setzen, wozu ihn K. einlud, hatte er keine Zeit – bat er K. um ein kurzes Gespräch unter vier Augen. »Es ist notwendig«, sagte er, mühselig schluckend, »zu meiner Beruhigung ist es notwendig.« K. schickte sofort die Diener aus dem Zimmer, mit der Weisung, niemand einzulassen. »Was habe ich gehört, Josef?« rief der Onkel, als sie allein waren, setzte sich auf den Tisch und stopfte unter sich, ohne hinzusehen, verschiedene Papiere, um besser zu sitzen. K. schwieg, er wußte, was kommen würde, aber, plötzlich von der anstrengenden Arbeit entspannt, wie er war, gab er sich zunächst einer angenehmen Mattigkeit hin und sah durch das Fenster auf die gegenüberliegende Straßenseite, von der von seinem Sitz aus nur ein kleiner, dreieckiger Ausschnitt zu sehen war, ein Stück leerer Häusermauer zwischen zwei Geschäftsauslagen. »Du schaust aus dem Fenster!« rief der Onkel mit erhobenen Armen, »um Himmels willen, Josef, antworte mir doch! Ist es wahr, kann es denn wahr sein?« »Lieber Onkel«, sagte K. und riß sich von seiner Zerstreutheit los, »ich weiß ja gar nicht, was du von mir willst.« »Josef«, sagte der Onkel warnend, »die Wahrheit hast du immer gesagt, soviel ich weiß. Soll ich deine letzten Worte als schlimmes Zeichen auffassen?« »Ich ahne ja, was du willst«, sagte K. folgsam, »du hast wahrscheinlich von meinem Prozeß gehört.« »So ist es«, antwortete der Onkel, langsam nickend, »ich habe von deinem Prozeß gehört.« »Von wem denn?« fragte K. »Erna hat es mir geschrieben«, sagte der Onkel, »sie hat ja keinen Verkehr mit dir, du kümmerst dich leider nicht viel um sie, trotzdem hat sie es erfahren. Heute habe ich den Brief bekommen und bin natürlich sofort hergefahren. Aus keinem anderen Grund, aber es scheint ein genügender Grund zu sein. Ich kann dir die Briefstelle, die dich betrifft, vorlesen.« Er zog den Brief aus der Brieftasche. »Hier ist es.« Sie schreibt: »Josef habe ich schon lange nicht gesehen, vorige Woche war ich einmal in der Bank, aber Josef war so beschäftigt, daß ich nicht vorgelassen wurde; ich habe fast eine Stunde gewartet, mußte dann aber nach Hause, weil ich Klavierstunde hatte. Ich hätte gern mit ihm gesprochen, vielleicht wird sich nächstens eine Gelegenheit finden. Zu meinem Namenstag hat er mir eine große Schachtel Schokolade geschickt, es war sehr lieb und aufmerksam. Ich hatte vergessen, es Euch damals zu schreiben, erst jetzt, da Ihr mich fragt, erinnere ich mich daran. Schokolade, müßt Ihr wissen, verschwindet nämlich in der Pension sofort, kaum ist man zum Bewußtsein dessen gekommen, daß man mit Schokolade beschenkt worden ist, ist sie auch schon weg. Aber was Josef betrifft, wollte ich Euch noch etwas sagen. Wie erwähnt, wurde ich in der Bank nicht zu ihm vorgelassen, weil er gerade mit einem Herrn verhandelte. Nachdem ich eine Zeitlang ruhig gewartet hatte, fragte ich einen Diener, ob die Verhandlung noch lange dauern werde. Er sagte, das dürfte wohl sein, denn es handle sich wahrscheinlich um den Prozeß, der gegen den Herrn Prokuristen geführt werde. Ich fragte, was denn das für ein Prozeß sei, ob er sich nicht irre, er aber sagte, er irre sich nicht, es sei ein Prozeß, und zwar ein schwerer Prozeß, mehr aber wisse er nicht. Er selbst möchte dem Herrn Prokuristen gerne helfen, denn dieser sei ein guter und gerechter Herr, aber er wisse nicht, wie er es anfangen sollte, und er möchte nur wünschen, daß sich einflußreiche Herren seiner annehmen würden. Dies werde auch sicher geschehen, und es werde schließlich ein gutes Ende nehmen, vorläufig aber stehe es, wie er aus der Laune des Herrn Prokuristen entnehmen könne, gar nicht gut. Ich legte diesen Reden natürlich nicht viel Bedeutung bei, suchte auch den einfältigen Diener zu beruhigen, verbot ihm, anderen gegenüber davon zu sprechen, und halte das Ganze für ein Geschwätz. Trotzdem wäre es vielleicht gut, wenn Du, liebster Vater, bei Deinem nächsten Besuch der Sache nachgehen wolltest, es wird Dir leicht sein, Genaueres zu erfahren und, wenn es wirklich nötig sein sollte, durch Deine großen, einflußreichen Bekanntschaften einzugreifen. Sollte es aber nicht nötig sein, was ja das wahrscheinlichste ist, so wird es wenigstens Deiner Tochter bald Gelegenheit geben, Dich zu umarmen, was sie freuen würde.‹ – Ein gutes Kind«, sagte der Onkel, als er die Vorlesung beendet hatte, und wischte einige Tränen aus den Augen fort. K. nickte, er hatte infolge der verschiedenen Störungen der letzten Zeit vollständig Erna vergessen, sogar ihren Geburtstag hatte er vergessen, und die Geschichte von der Schokolade war offenbar nur zu dem Zweck erfunden, um ihn vor Onkel und Tante in Schutz zu nehmen. Es war sehr rührend, und mit den Theaterkarten, die er ihr von jetzt ab regelmäßig schicken wollte, gewiß nicht genügend belohnt, aber zu Besuchen in der Pension und zu Unterhaltungen mit einer kleinen achtzehnjährigen Gymnasiastin fühlte er sich jetzt nicht geeignet. »Und was sagst du jetzt?« fragte der Onkel, der durch den Brief alle Eile und Aufregung vergessen hatte und ihn noch einmal zu lesen schien. »Ja, Onkel«, sagte K., »es ist wahr.« »Wahr?« rief der Onkel.

source_text: Gleich nach der Begrüßung – sich in den Fauteuil zu setzen, wozu ihn K. einlud, hatte er keine Zeit – bat er K. um ein kurzes Gespräch unter vier Augen. »Es ist notwendig«, sagte er, mühselig schluckend, »zu meiner Beruhigung ist es notwendig.« K. schickte sofort die Diener aus dem Zimmer, mit der Weisung, niemand einzulassen. »Was habe ich gehört, Josef?« rief der Onkel, als sie allein waren, setzte sich auf den Tisch und stopfte unter sich, ohne hinzusehen, verschiedene Papiere, um besser zu sitzen. K. schwieg, er wußte, was kommen würde, aber, plötzlich von der anstrengenden Arbeit entspannt, wie er war, gab er sich zunächst einer angenehmen Mattigkeit hin und sah durch das Fenster auf die gegenüberliegende Straßenseite, von der von seinem Sitz aus nur ein kleiner, dreieckiger Ausschnitt zu sehen war, ein Stück leerer Häusermauer zwischen zwei Geschäftsauslagen. »Du schaust aus dem Fenster!« rief der Onkel mit erhobenen Armen, »um Himmels willen, Josef, antworte mir doch! Ist es wahr, kann es denn wahr sein?« »Lieber Onkel«, sagte K. und riß sich von seiner Zerstreutheit los, »ich weiß ja gar nicht, was du von mir willst.« »Josef«, sagte der Onkel warnend, »die Wahrheit hast du immer gesagt, soviel ich weiß. Soll ich deine letzten Worte als schlimmes Zeichen auffassen?« »Ich ahne ja, was du willst«, sagte K. folgsam, »du hast wahrscheinlich von meinem Prozeß gehört.« »So ist es«, antwortete der Onkel, langsam nickend, »ich habe von deinem Prozeß gehört.« »Von wem denn?« fragte K. »Erna hat es mir geschrieben«, sagte der Onkel, »sie hat ja keinen Verkehr mit dir, du kümmerst dich leider nicht viel um sie, trotzdem hat sie es erfahren. Heute habe ich den Brief bekommen und bin natürlich sofort hergefahren. Aus keinem anderen Grund, aber es scheint ein genügender Grund zu sein. Ich kann dir die Briefstelle, die dich betrifft, vorlesen.« Er zog den Brief aus der Brieftasche. »Hier ist es.« Sie schreibt: »Josef habe ich schon lange nicht gesehen, vorige Woche war ich einmal in der Bank, aber Josef war so beschäftigt, daß ich nicht vorgelassen wurde; ich habe fast eine Stunde gewartet, mußte dann aber nach Hause, weil ich Klavierstunde hatte. Ich hätte gern mit ihm gesprochen, vielleicht wird sich nächstens eine Gelegenheit finden. Zu meinem Namenstag hat er mir eine große Schachtel Schokolade geschickt, es war sehr lieb und aufmerksam. Ich hatte vergessen, es Euch damals zu schreiben, erst jetzt, da Ihr mich fragt, erinnere ich mich daran. Schokolade, müßt Ihr wissen, verschwindet nämlich in der Pension sofort, kaum ist man zum Bewußtsein dessen gekommen, daß man mit Schokolade beschenkt worden ist, ist sie auch schon weg. Aber was Josef betrifft, wollte ich Euch noch etwas sagen. Wie erwähnt, wurde ich in der Bank nicht zu ihm vorgelassen, weil er gerade mit einem Herrn verhandelte. Nachdem ich eine Zeitlang ruhig gewartet hatte, fragte ich einen Diener, ob die Verhandlung noch lange dauern werde. Er sagte, das dürfte wohl sein, denn es handle sich wahrscheinlich um den Prozeß, der gegen den Herrn Prokuristen geführt werde. Ich fragte, was denn das für ein Prozeß sei, ob er sich nicht irre, er aber sagte, er irre sich nicht, es sei ein Prozeß, und zwar ein schwerer Prozeß, mehr aber wisse er nicht. Er selbst möchte dem Herrn Prokuristen gerne helfen, denn dieser sei ein guter und gerechter Herr, aber er wisse nicht, wie er es anfangen sollte, und er möchte nur wünschen, daß sich einflußreiche Herren seiner annehmen würden. Dies werde auch sicher geschehen, und es werde schließlich ein gutes Ende nehmen, vorläufig aber stehe es, wie er aus der Laune des Herrn Prokuristen entnehmen könne, gar nicht gut. Ich legte diesen Reden natürlich nicht viel Bedeutung bei, suchte auch den einfältigen Diener zu beruhigen, verbot ihm, anderen gegenüber davon zu sprechen, und halte das Ganze für ein Geschwätz. Trotzdem wäre es vielleicht gut, wenn Du, liebster Vater, bei Deinem nächsten Besuch der Sache nachgehen wolltest, es wird Dir leicht sein, Genaueres zu erfahren und, wenn es wirklich nötig sein sollte, durch Deine großen, einflußreichen Bekanntschaften einzugreifen. Sollte es aber nicht nötig sein, was ja das wahrscheinlichste ist, so wird es wenigstens Deiner Tochter bald Gelegenheit geben, Dich zu umarmen, was sie freuen würde.‹ – Ein gutes Kind«, sagte der Onkel, als er die Vorlesung beendet hatte, und wischte einige Tränen aus den Augen fort. K. nickte, er hatte infolge der verschiedenen Störungen der letzten Zeit vollständig Erna vergessen, sogar ihren Geburtstag hatte er vergessen, und die Geschichte von der Schokolade war offenbar nur zu dem Zweck erfunden, um ihn vor Onkel und Tante in Schutz zu nehmen. Es war sehr rührend, und mit den Theaterkarten, die er ihr von jetzt ab regelmäßig schicken wollte, gewiß nicht genügend belohnt, aber zu Besuchen in der Pension und zu Unterhaltungen mit einer kleinen achtzehnjährigen Gymnasiastin fühlte er sich jetzt nicht geeignet. »Und was sagst du jetzt?« fragte der Onkel, der durch den Brief alle Eile und Aufregung vergessen hatte und ihn noch einmal zu lesen schien. »Ja, Onkel«, sagte K., »es ist wahr.« »Wahr?« rief der Onkel.

translation: — Ah, yes, that's Derebin's place. Imagine, Derebin's so lucky: his aunt got into a fight with her son because he married a serf, and now she's disinherited him. I often think to myself, what a treasure it would be to have an aunt like that in reserve for the future! And what's with you, brother, have you gone off into the woods? Of course, I know you're often busy with your learned pursuits, and you love reading (why in the world would Nozdrev have concluded that our hero is involved with scholarly pursuits and enjoys reading, we can hardly say as much about ourselves, and much less about Chichikov). Oh, brother Chichikov, if only you could see... why, there would be a feast for your satirical mind (why Chichikov had a satirical mind, we can't say either). Imagine, brother, at Likhachiov's place, they were playing sleds, oh, that was a laugh! And Perepenedev, who was with me, said, "Just imagine, if only Chichikov were there, ha!... " (though, as a matter of fact, Chichikov had never even heard of Perepenedev). Come on, admit it, brother, you were pretty unkind to me then, remember when we played checkers, I won... Yes, brother, you flat-out cheated me. But, heavens know, I'm not the type to hold a grudge. The other day with the president... Ah, yes! I almost forgot to tell you that in the city, everyone's against you; they think you're printing fake paper, they've been bothering me, but I stuck up for you, told them we were classmates and I knew your father; well, there's no need to go on, I gave them a real earful.
source_text: — Да, точно, это у Деребина Вахрамей. Вообрази, Деребину какое счастье: тетка его поссорилась с сыном за то, что женился на крепостной, и теперь записала ему все именье. Я думаю себе, вот если бы эдакую тетку иметь для дальнейших! Да что ты, брат, так отдалился от всех, нигде не бываешь? Конечно, я знаю, что ты занят иногда учеными предметами, любишь читать (уж почему Ноздрев заключил, что герой наш занимается учеными предметами и любит почитать, этого, признаемся, мы никак не можем сказать, а Чичиков и того менее). Ах, брат Чичиков, если бы ты только увидал… вот уж, точно, была бы пища твоему сатирическому уму (почему у Чичикова был сатирический ум, это тоже неизвестно). Вообрази, брат, у купца Лихачева играли в горку, вот уж где смех был! Перепендев, который был со мною: «Вот, говорит, если бы теперь Чичиков, уж вот бы ему точно!..» (между тем Чичиков отроду не знал никакого Перепендева). They think that you’re turning out counterfeit bank notes; they started pestering me, but I stood up for you as firm as a rock; I told ’em a great deal about you, that I’d gone to school with you and had known your father. Well, there’s no use talking even , I spun them a fine yarn.”

translation: The guests continued to stare in amazement, whisper to each other, and exchange glances, but it soon became clear that all this was pre-planned and staged, and that Nastasya Filippovna, despite her having, of course, gone quite mad, was now untouchable. Everyone was tortured by an unbearable curiosity. At the same time, there was no one left to be afraid of. There were only two women: bold and worldly Darya Alexeievna, whom it was hard to embarrass, and the beautiful but quiet stranger. But the quiet stranger was unlikely to grasp anything; she was a foreign visitor and knew no Russian, and besides, she seemed to be as stupid as she was beautiful. She was new to society and was already accustomed to being invited to smart parties, dressed up like a doll, and placed there like a pretty picture to decorate the evening - just as some people gather a painting, vase, statue, or screen from their acquaintances for a single evening. As for the men, Pticyn was on good terms with Rogozhin, Ferdyshchenko was at home among them; Ganin was still getting over his initial shock, but he was powerless to resist the burning urge to reach the end of his shameful situation; the old teacher, who didn't understand what was going on, was almost crying and trembling with fear, noticing some extraordinary excitement around and in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he adored as his grandchild; but he would rather die than leave her at such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, he could not compromise himself in such adventures, but he was too interested in the business, though it had taken a completely mad turn; and Nastasya Filippovna had dropped a few words on him, impossible to ignore, not to mention explaining the situation. He decided to see it through to the end and remain completely silent, just observing, which, of course, was consistent with his dignity. Only General Yepanchin, still smarting from the hasty and ridiculous return of the gift, could now be even more offended by all these extraordinary eccentricities or, for example, Rogozhin's arrival; and, as a man of his standing, he had already sunk too low by deciding to sit next to Pticyn and Ferdyshchenko; but what passion could do, could finally be defeated by a sense of duty, the feeling of obligation, dignity, and importance, and generally self-respect, so that Rogozhin and company were simply impossible in his presence.
source_text: Гости продолжали изумляться, шептаться и переглядываться, но стало совершенно ясно, что всё это было рассчитано и устроено заранее и что Настасью Филипповну, — хоть она и, конечно, с ума сошла, — теперь не собьешь. Всех мучило ужасно любопытство. Притом же и пугаться-то очень было некому. Дам было только две: Дарья Алексеевна, барыня бойкая и видавшая всякие виды и которую трудно было сконфузить, и прекрасная, но молчаливая незнакомка. Но молчаливая незнакомка вряд ли что и понять могла: это была приезжая немка и русского языка ничего не знала; кроме того, кажется, была столько же глупа, сколько и прекрасна. Она была внове, и уже принято было приглашать ее на известные вечера, в пышнейшем костюме, причесанную как на выставку, и сажать как прелестную картинку для того, чтобы скрасить вечер, — точно так, как иные добывают для своих вечеров у знакомых, на один раз, картину, вазу, статую или экран. Что же касается мужчин, то Птицын, например, был приятель с Рогожиным, Фердыщенко был как рыба в воде; Ганечка всё еще в себя прийти не мог, но хоть смутно, а неудержимо сам ощущал горячечную потребность достоять до конца у своего позорного столба; старичок учитель, мало понимавший в чем дело, чуть не плакал и буквально дрожал от страха, заметив какую-то необыкновенную тревогу кругом и в Настасье Филипповне, которую обожал, как свою внучку; но он скорее бы умер, чем ее в такую минуту покинул. Что же касается Афанасия Ивановича, то, конечно, он себя компрометировать в таких приключениях не мог; но он слишком был заинтересован в деле, хотя бы и принимавшем такой сумасшедший оборот; да и Настасья Филипповна выронила на его счет два-три словечка таких, что уехать никак нельзя было, не разъяснив окончательно дела. Он решился досидеть до конца и уже совершенно замолчать и оставаться лишь наблюдателем, что, конечно, и требовалось его достоинством. Один лишь генерал Епанчин, только что сейчас пред этим разобиженный таким бесцеремонным и смешным возвратом ему подарка, конечно, еще более мог теперь обидеться всеми этими необыкновенными эксцентричностями или, например, появлением Рогожина; да и человек, как он, и без того уже слишком снизошел, решившись сесть рядом с Птицыным и Фердыщенком; но что могла сделать сила страсти, то могло быть, наконец, побеждено чувством обязанности, ощущением долга, чина и значения и вообще уважением к себе, так что Рогожин с компанией, во всяком случае в присутствии его превосходительства, был невозможен.

human_translations.translator_1: The guests continued to express their amazement, to whisper and exchange glances, but it transpired that all this had been worked out and arranged in advance by Nastasya Filippovna, who though she had clearly lost her mind was not to be swayed from her decision. Everyone was dying of curiosity. Besides, there was no one there who would be easily frightened. There were only two ladies: Darya Alexeyevna, a lady who had seen life and who could not be easily upset, and the gorgeous, but silent, stranger. But the latter had little idea of what was going on anyway; she was a German visitor and didn’t know a word of Russian; besides, she appeared to be as dumb as she was beautiful. She was quite a new arrival on the scene, but it had already become customary to invite her to certain soirées. Decked out in some dazzling outfit, her hair arranged with marvellous ingenuity, she was displayed as some magnificently decorative picture – precisely the way people do in fact borrow a painting, a vase, a statue or a screen from friends for just one night. As for the men, Ptitsyn for instance was Rogozhin’s friend; Ferdyshchenko was clearly in his element; Ganya was still agitated but, however vaguely, felt an irrepressible compulsion to endure to the very end the ignominy of his situation; the old schoolmaster, who had scant understanding of what was going on around him and sensed an unusual excitation centred on Nastasya Filippovna, whom he adored as his own granddaughter, was close to tears and positively trembling with fright, but he would rather have expired on the spot than leave the gathering at that particular moment. As regards Afanasy Ivanovich, he of course could not afford to compromise himself in such adventures; but he was already too much involved in the proceedings in spite of them having taken such a bizarre turn; besides, Nastasya Filippovna had dropped one or two personal remarks in consequence of which it was quite impossible for him to leave without seeking a final clarification. He therefore decided to sit it out to the end merely as an observer without saying a single word, which of course accorded well with his dignity. That left only the General, whose gift had just been so unceremoniously and risibly returned to him. He may have had yet other and weightier excuses to feel offended, namely all the outlandish goings-on, not least the imminent appearance of Rogozhin; in any case, he had already conceded far too much by consenting to share the same space with Ptitsyn and Ferdyshchenko; but if his infatuation had so misled him, it could well be compensated by his sense of duty, his status and overall dignity, such that the presence of Rogozhin and his companions in the company of His Highness was quite unthinkable.
human_translations.translator_2: The guests continued to show bewilderment, whisper and exchange glances, but it became perfectly clear that all this had been calculated and arranged beforehand and that Nastasya Filippovna — although she had, of course, taken leave of her senses — would not be deflected from her course. They were all racked with curiosity. Moreover, no one there was likely to be too intimidated. There were only two ladies: Darya Alexeyevna, the pert lady, who had seen all manner of things and would be hard to disconcert, and the beautiful, but silent stranger. But the silent stranger would hardly understand anything: she was a visiting German, and knew nothing of the Russian language; in addition, she seemed to be as stupid as she was beautiful. She was new here, and it was already the accepted thing to invite her to certain soirees, in the most extravagant attire, with her hair done up as for a fashion show, and have her sit like a charming picture in order to adorn the soiree in just the same way as some people obtain from friends, for a single evening, a picture, a vase, a statue or a screen in order to adorn their soirees. As for the men, Ptitsyn, for example, was a friend of Rogozhin’s; Ferdyshchenko was like a fish in water; Ganechka was still unable to pull himself together, but had a dim though irresistible sense of the need for him to stand at his pillory to the end; the old schoolmaster, who had little idea of what it was all about, was very nearly in tears and literally trembled with fear as he noticed the extraordinary state of anxiety in those around him and in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he worshipped like his grandchild; but he would rather have died than abandon her at such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, he could not, of course, compromise himself with such adventures; but he had too much at stake in the matter, even though it had taken such a crazy turn; and in any case, Nastasya Filippovna had dropped a few remarks in his regard which had been such that it would be impossible for him to leave without having finally cleared up the matter. He resolved to stay to the end and keep silent altogether, remaining solely as an observer, something that was, of course, demanded by his dignity. Only General Yepanchin, who had just before this been deeply insulted by the unceremonious and ridiculous return of his present to him, might possibly be even more insulted by all these extraordinary eccentricities or, for example, by Rogozhin’s arrival; and indeed a man like him had already sunk low enough by bringing himself to sit beside Ptitsyn and Ferdyshchenko; but what the power of passion was able to do was, at last, overcome by a feeling of obligation, a sense of duty, rank and self-respect, so that Rogozhin and his company, in his excellency’s presence, at any rate, were out of the question.
human_translations.translator_3: The guests went on being amazed, whispering and exchanging glances, but it became perfectly clear that it had all been calculated and arranged beforehand, and that now Nastasya Filippovna—though she was, of course, out of her mind—would not be thrown off. They all suffered terribly from curiosity. Besides, there was really no one to be frightened. There were only two ladies: Darya Alexeevna, the sprightly lady, who had seen everything and whom it would have been very hard to put out, and the beautiful but silent stranger. But the silent stranger was scarcely able to understand anything: she was a traveling German lady and did not know a word of Russian; besides that, it seems she was as stupid as she was beautiful. She was a novelty, and it was an accepted thing to invite her to certain evenings, in magnificent costume, her hair done up as if for an exhibition, and to sit her there like a lovely picture to adorn the evening, just as some people, for their evenings, borrow some painting, vase, statue, or screen from their friends for one time only. As far as the men were concerned, Ptitsyn, for instance, was friends with Rogozhin; Ferdyshchenko was like a fish in water; Ganechka had not yet come to his senses, but felt vaguely yet irresistibly the feverish need to stand in this pillory to the end; the old schoolteacher, who had little grasp of what was going on, all but wept and literally trembled with fear, noticing some sort of extraordinary alarm around him and in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he doted on like a granddaughter; but he would sooner have died than abandon her at such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, he, of course, could not compromise himself in such adventures; but he was much too interested in the affair, even if it had taken such a crazy turn; then, too, Nastasya Filippovna had dropped two or three such little phrases on his account, that he could by no means leave without clarifying the matter definitively. He resolved to sit it out to the end and now to be completely silent and remain only as an observer, which, of course, his dignity demanded. General Epanchin alone, thoroughly offended as he had just been by such an unceremonious and ridiculous return of his present, could, of course, be still more offended now by all these extraordinary eccentricities or, for instance, by the appearance of Rogozhin; then, too, even without that, a man like him had already condescended too much by resolving to sit down beside Ptitsyn and Ferdyshchenko; but what the power of passion could do, could also be overcome in the end by a feeling of responsibility, a sense of duty, rank, and importance, and generally of self-respect, so that Rogozhin and his company, in his excellency’s presence at any rate, were impossible.
human_translations.translator_4: The guests exchanged glances; they were annoyed and bewildered by the episode; but it was clear enough that all this had been pre-arranged and expected by Nastasia Philipovna, and that there was no use in trying to stop her now —for she was little short of insane. Besides, they were naturally inquisitive to see what was to happen. There was nobody who would be likely to feel much alarm. There were but two ladies present; one of whom was the lively actress, who was not easily frightened, and the other the silent German beauty who, it turned out, did not understand a word of Russian, and seemed to be as stupid as she was lovely. Her acquaintances invited her to their "At Homes" because she was so decorative. She was exhibited to their guests like a valuable picture, or vase, or statue, or firescreen. As for the men, Ptitsin was one of Rogojin's friends; Ferdishenko was as much at home as a fish in the sea, Gania, not yet recovered from his amazement, appeared to be chained to a pillory. The old professor did not in the least understand what was happening; but when he noticed how extremely agitated the mistress of the house, and her friends, seemed, he nearly wept, and trembled with fright: but he would rather have died than leave Nastasia Philipovna at such a crisis, for he loved her as if she were his own granddaughter. Afanasy Ivanovitch greatly disliked having anything to do with the affair, but he was too much interested to leave, in spite of the mad turn things had taken; and a few words that had dropped from the lips of Nastasia puzzled him so much, that he felt he could not go without an explanation. He resolved therefore, to see it out, and to adopt the attitude of silent spectator, as most suited to his dignity. Genera Epanchin alone determined to depart. He was annoyed at the manner in which his gift had been returned, an though he had condescended, under the influence of passion, to place himself on a level with Ptitsin and Ferdishenko, his self-respect and sense of duty now returned together with a consciousness of what was due to his social rank and official importance. In short, he plainly showed his conviction that a man in his position could have nothing to do with Rogojin and his companions.

translation: The guests continued to marvel, whisper and exchange glances, but it became patently clear that everything had been calculated and planned in advance, and that Nastasya Filipovna, though she was indeed out of her mind, was not to be trifled with. Everyone was consumed with a terrible curiosity. It must be noted that there was also no one to be frightened of: there were only two women, Darya Alexeievna, a lively woman who had seen a lot and was hard to shock, and the beautiful, but silent, foreigner. The silent foreigner, however, could hardly be expected to understand anything: she was a German visitor and did not know a word of Russian; besides, it seemed she was as foolish as she was beautiful. She had arrived recently, and it had already become customary to invite her to respectable gatherings, dressed up to the nines, coiffed like a porcelain figurine, and placed there like a pretty decoration to enliven the evening - just as some people procure, on one occasion, a picture, vase, statue or a screen from their acquaintances. As for the men, Ptilitsyn was on friendly terms with Rostov, Firshtenka was as at home as a fish in water, Ganenka was still trying to get a grip on himself, but despite his confused state, felt an irrepressible burning need to get to the end of his shameful ordeal; the old teacher, who didn't quite understand what was happening, was on the verge of tears and literally shuddered with fear, noticing the extraordinary agitation around and in Nastasya Filipovna, whom he adored like a granddaughter; but he would rather die than leave her at such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, he, of course, could not compromise himself in such escapades, but he was too intrigued by the affair, despite its utterly absurd turn; and Nastasya Filipovna had dropped a few remarks about him that made it impossible for him to leave without clarifying the matter. He decided to stick it out to the end, remaining silent and merely an observer, which, of course, suited his dignity. Only General Epanchin, who had just been offended by such an unceremonious and ridiculous rejection of his gift, could now only take umbrage at these incredible eccentricities or, for instance, Rostov's appearance; and as a man of his standing, who had already sunk low by deciding to sit with Ptilitsyn and Firshtenka, he was not likely to put up with Rostov and company, even more so in the presence of such an esteemed personage.

source_text: Гости продолжали изумляться, шептаться и переглядываться, но стало совершенно ясно, что всё это было рассчитано и устроено заранее и что Настасью Филипповну, — хоть она и, конечно, с ума сошла, — теперь не собьешь. Всех мучило ужасно любопытство. Притом же и пугаться-то очень было некому. Дам было только две: Дарья Алексеевна, барыня бойкая и видавшая всякие виды и которую трудно было сконфузить, и прекрасная, но молчаливая незнакомка. Но молчаливая незнакомка вряд ли что и понять могла: это была приезжая немка и русского языка ничего не знала; кроме того, кажется, была столько же глупа, сколько и прекрасна. Она была внове, и уже принято было приглашать ее на известные вечера, в пышнейшем костюме, причесанную как на выставку, и сажать как прелестную картинку для того, чтобы скрасить вечер, — точно так, как иные добывают для своих вечеров у знакомых, на один раз, картину, вазу, статую или экран. Что же касается мужчин, то Птицын, например, был приятель с Рогожиным, Фердыщенко был как рыба в воде; Ганечка всё еще в себя прийти не мог, но хоть смутно, а неудержимо сам ощущал горячечную потребность достоять до конца у своего позорного столба; старичок учитель, мало понимавший в чем дело, чуть не плакал и буквально дрожал от страха, заметив какую-то необыкновенную тревогу кругом и в Настасье Филипповне, которую обожал, как свою внучку; но он скорее бы умер, чем ее в такую минуту покинул. Что же касается Афанасия Ивановича, то, конечно, он себя компрометировать в таких приключениях не мог; но он слишком был заинтересован в деле, хотя бы и принимавшем такой сумасшедший оборот; да и Настасья Филипповна выронила на его счет два-три словечка таких, что уехать никак нельзя было, не разъяснив окончательно дела. Он решился досидеть до конца и уже совершенно замолчать и оставаться лишь наблюдателем, что, конечно, и требовалось его достоинством. Один лишь генерал Епанчин, только что сейчас пред этим разобиженный таким бесцеремонным и смешным возвратом ему подарка, конечно, еще более мог теперь обидеться всеми этими необыкновенными эксцентричностями или, например, появлением Рогожина; да и человек, как он, и без того уже слишком снизошел, решившись сесть рядом с Птицыным и Фердыщенком; но что могла сделать сила страсти, то могло быть, наконец, побеждено чувством обязанности, ощущением долга, чина и значения и вообще уважением к себе, так что Рогожин с компанией, во всяком случае в присутствии его превосходительства, был невозможен.
gt_translation: The guests continued to be amazed, whispering and exchanging glances, but it became quite clear that all this had been calculated and arranged in advance and that Nastasya Filippovna, although she, of course, had gone mad, could not be fooled now. Everyone was tormented by terribly curiosity. Moreover, there was no one to be afraid of. There were only two ladies: Darya Alekseevna, a brisk lady who had seen all sorts of things and was difficult to embarrass, and a beautiful but silent stranger. But the silent stranger could hardly understand anything: she was a visiting German woman and knew nothing of the Russian language; besides, she seems to have been as stupid as she was beautiful. She was new, and it was already customary to invite her to famous evenings, in the most magnificent costume, combed as if for an exhibition, and planted like a lovely picture in order to brighten up the evening - just like others get for their evenings from acquaintances, for one times, a picture, a vase, a statue or a screen. As for the men, Ptitsyn, for example, was a friend with Rogozhin, Ferdyshchenko was like a fish in water; Ganechka still could not come to his senses, but even vaguely, but irresistibly, he himself felt a feverish need to endure to the end at his pillory; the old teacher, who had little understanding of what was happening, almost wept and literally trembled with fear, noticing some unusual anxiety around and in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he adored like his granddaughter; but he would rather die than leave her at such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, then, of course, he could not compromise himself in such adventures; but he was too interested in the matter, even if it took such a crazy turn; and Nastasya Filippovna dropped two or three words at his expense, such that it was impossible to leave without finally explaining the matter. He decided to sit through to the end and completely shut up and remain only an observer, which, of course, was required by his dignity. Only General Yepanchin, just now offended by such an unceremonious and ridiculous return of a gift to him, of course, could now be even more offended by all these unusual eccentricities or, for example, the appearance of Rogozhin; and a man like him had already condescended too much, having decided to sit next to Ptitsyn and Ferdyshchenko; but what the force of passion could do could be finally defeated by a sense of duty, a sense of duty, rank and importance, and generally self-respect, so that Rogozhin with company, at least in the presence of his Excellency, was impossible.

human_translations.translator_1: The guests continued to express their amazement, to whisper and exchange glances, but it transpired that all this had been worked out and arranged in advance by Nastasya Filippovna, who though she had clearly lost her mind was not to be swayed from her decision. Everyone was dying of curiosity. Besides, there was no one there who would be easily frightened. There were only two ladies: Darya Alexeyevna, a lady who had seen life and who could not be easily upset, and the gorgeous, but silent, stranger. But the latter had little idea of what was going on anyway; she was a German visitor and didn’t know a word of Russian; besides, she appeared to be as dumb as she was beautiful. She was quite a new arrival on the scene, but it had already become customary to invite her to certain soirées. Decked out in some dazzling outfit, her hair arranged with marvellous ingenuity, she was displayed as some magnificently decorative picture – precisely the way people do in fact borrow a painting, a vase, a statue or a screen from friends for just one night. As for the men, Ptitsyn for instance was Rogozhin’s friend; Ferdyshchenko was clearly in his element; Ganya was still agitated but, however vaguely, felt an irrepressible compulsion to endure to the very end the ignominy of his situation; the old schoolmaster, who had scant understanding of what was going on around him and sensed an unusual excitation centred on Nastasya Filippovna, whom he adored as his own granddaughter, was close to tears and positively trembling with fright, but he would rather have expired on the spot than leave the gathering at that particular moment. As regards Afanasy Ivanovich, he of course could not afford to compromise himself in such adventures; but he was already too much involved in the proceedings in spite of them having taken such a bizarre turn; besides, Nastasya Filippovna had dropped one or two personal remarks in consequence of which it was quite impossible for him to leave without seeking a final clarification. He therefore decided to sit it out to the end merely as an observer without saying a single word, which of course accorded well with his dignity. That left only the General, whose gift had just been so unceremoniously and risibly returned to him. He may have had yet other and weightier excuses to feel offended, namely all the outlandish goings-on, not least the imminent appearance of Rogozhin; in any case, he had already conceded far too much by consenting to share the same space with Ptitsyn and Ferdyshchenko; but if his infatuation had so misled him, it could well be compensated by his sense of duty, his status and overall dignity, such that the presence of Rogozhin and his companions in the company of His Highness was quite unthinkable.
human_translations.translator_2: The guests continued to show bewilderment, whisper and exchange glances, but it became perfectly clear that all this had been calculated and arranged beforehand and that Nastasya Filippovna — although she had, of course, taken leave of her senses — would not be deflected from her course. They were all racked with curiosity. Moreover, no one there was likely to be too intimidated. There were only two ladies: Darya Alexeyevna, the pert lady, who had seen all manner of things and would be hard to disconcert, and the beautiful, but silent stranger. But the silent stranger would hardly understand anything: she was a visiting German, and knew nothing of the Russian language; in addition, she seemed to be as stupid as she was beautiful. She was new here, and it was already the accepted thing to invite her to certain soirees, in the most extravagant attire, with her hair done up as for a fashion show, and have her sit like a charming picture in order to adorn the soiree in just the same way as some people obtain from friends, for a single evening, a picture, a vase, a statue or a screen in order to adorn their soirees. As for the men, Ptitsyn, for example, was a friend of Rogozhin’s; Ferdyshchenko was like a fish in water; Ganechka was still unable to pull himself together, but had a dim though irresistible sense of the need for him to stand at his pillory to the end; the old schoolmaster, who had little idea of what it was all about, was very nearly in tears and literally trembled with fear as he noticed the extraordinary state of anxiety in those around him and in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he worshipped like his grandchild; but he would rather have died than abandon her at such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, he could not, of course, compromise himself with such adventures; but he had too much at stake in the matter, even though it had taken such a crazy turn; and in any case, Nastasya Filippovna had dropped a few remarks in his regard which had been such that it would be impossible for him to leave without having finally cleared up the matter. He resolved to stay to the end and keep silent altogether, remaining solely as an observer, something that was, of course, demanded by his dignity. Only General Yepanchin, who had just before this been deeply insulted by the unceremonious and ridiculous return of his present to him, might possibly be even more insulted by all these extraordinary eccentricities or, for example, by Rogozhin’s arrival; and indeed a man like him had already sunk low enough by bringing himself to sit beside Ptitsyn and Ferdyshchenko; but what the power of passion was able to do was, at last, overcome by a feeling of obligation, a sense of duty, rank and self-respect, so that Rogozhin and his company, in his excellency’s presence, at any rate, were out of the question.
human_translations.translator_3: The guests went on being amazed, whispering and exchanging glances, but it became perfectly clear that it had all been calculated and arranged beforehand, and that now Nastasya Filippovna—though she was, of course, out of her mind—would not be thrown off. They all suffered terribly from curiosity. Besides, there was really no one to be frightened. There were only two ladies: Darya Alexeevna, the sprightly lady, who had seen everything and whom it would have been very hard to put out, and the beautiful but silent stranger. But the silent stranger was scarcely able to understand anything: she was a traveling German lady and did not know a word of Russian; besides that, it seems she was as stupid as she was beautiful. She was a novelty, and it was an accepted thing to invite her to certain evenings, in magnificent costume, her hair done up as if for an exhibition, and to sit her there like a lovely picture to adorn the evening, just as some people, for their evenings, borrow some painting, vase, statue, or screen from their friends for one time only. As far as the men were concerned, Ptitsyn, for instance, was friends with Rogozhin; Ferdyshchenko was like a fish in water; Ganechka had not yet come to his senses, but felt vaguely yet irresistibly the feverish need to stand in this pillory to the end; the old schoolteacher, who had little grasp of what was going on, all but wept and literally trembled with fear, noticing some sort of extraordinary alarm around him and in Nastasya Filippovna, whom he doted on like a granddaughter; but he would sooner have died than abandon her at such a moment. As for Afanasy Ivanovich, he, of course, could not compromise himself in such adventures; but he was much too interested in the affair, even if it had taken such a crazy turn; then, too, Nastasya Filippovna had dropped two or three such little phrases on his account, that he could by no means leave without clarifying the matter definitively. He resolved to sit it out to the end and now to be completely silent and remain only as an observer, which, of course, his dignity demanded. General Epanchin alone, thoroughly offended as he had just been by such an unceremonious and ridiculous return of his present, could, of course, be still more offended now by all these extraordinary eccentricities or, for instance, by the appearance of Rogozhin; then, too, even without that, a man like him had already condescended too much by resolving to sit down beside Ptitsyn and Ferdyshchenko; but what the power of passion could do, could also be overcome in the end by a feeling of responsibility, a sense of duty, rank, and importance, and generally of self-respect, so that Rogozhin and his company, in his excellency’s presence at any rate, were impossible.
human_translations.translator_4: The guests exchanged glances; they were annoyed and bewildered by the episode; but it was clear enough that all this had been pre-arranged and expected by Nastasia Philipovna, and that there was no use in trying to stop her now —for she was little short of insane. Besides, they were naturally inquisitive to see what was to happen. There was nobody who would be likely to feel much alarm. There were but two ladies present; one of whom was the lively actress, who was not easily frightened, and the other the silent German beauty who, it turned out, did not understand a word of Russian, and seemed to be as stupid as she was lovely. Her acquaintances invited her to their "At Homes" because she was so decorative. She was exhibited to their guests like a valuable picture, or vase, or statue, or firescreen. As for the men, Ptitsin was one of Rogojin's friends; Ferdishenko was as much at home as a fish in the sea, Gania, not yet recovered from his amazement, appeared to be chained to a pillory. The old professor did not in the least understand what was happening; but when he noticed how extremely agitated the mistress of the house, and her friends, seemed, he nearly wept, and trembled with fright: but he would rather have died than leave Nastasia Philipovna at such a crisis, for he loved her as if she were his own granddaughter. Afanasy Ivanovitch greatly disliked having anything to do with the affair, but he was too much interested to leave, in spite of the mad turn things had taken; and a few words that had dropped from the lips of Nastasia puzzled him so much, that he felt he could not go without an explanation. He resolved therefore, to see it out, and to adopt the attitude of silent spectator, as most suited to his dignity. Genera Epanchin alone determined to depart. He was annoyed at the manner in which his gift had been returned, an though he had condescended, under the influence of passion, to place himself on a level with Ptitsin and Ferdishenko, his self-respect and sense of duty now returned together with a consciousness of what was due to his social rank and official importance. In short, he plainly showed his conviction that a man in his position could have nothing to do with Rogojin and his companions.

Everyone was wracked with extraordinary curiosity. Moreover, it was now impossible to be afraid; there were only two women present: the lively and experienced Mrs. Dar'ya Alekseyevna, who was not easily flustered, and the beautiful, but taciturn stranger. However, it was unlikely that the stranger could even understand what was happening: she was a foreigner, didn't speak Russian, and appeared to be just as stupid as she was beautiful. She had been in town for some time, and it was already a habit to invite her to various gatherings, dress her up in her finest clothes, style her hair like a work of art, and put her on display like a decorative picture to brighten up the evening, just as some people collect paintings, vases, statues, or screens for their own parties.
