source_text: — Довольно, господин Терентьев, довольно, — удалось перебить Гавриле Ардалионовичу, — успокойтесь, не раздражайте себя; вы, кажется, очень нездоровы? Я вам сочувствую. В таком случае, если хотите, я кончил, то есть принужден буду сообщить только вкратце те факты, которые, по моему убеждению, не лишнее было бы узнать во всей полноте, — прибавил он, заметив некоторое всеобщее движение, похожее на нетерпение. — Я желаю только сообщить, с доказательствами, для сведения всех заинтересованных в деле, что ваша матушка, господин Бурдовский, потому единственно пользовалась расположением и заботливостью о ней Павлищева, что была родною сестрой той дворовой девушки, в которую Николай Андреевич Павлищев был влюблен в самой первой своей молодости, но до того, что непременно бы женился на ней, если б она не умерла скоропостижно. Я имею доказательства, что этот семейный факт, совершенно точный и верный, весьма малоизвестен, даже совсем забыт. Далее я бы мог объяснить, как ваша матушка еще десятилетним ребенком была взята господином Павлищевым на воспитание вместо родственницы, что ей отложено было значительное приданое и что все эти заботы породили чрезвычайно тревожные слухи между многочисленною родней Павлищева; думали даже, что он женится на своей воспитаннице, но кончилось тем, что она вышла по склонности (и это я точнейшим образом мог бы доказать) за межевого чиновника, господина Бурдовского, на двадцатом году своего возраста. Тут у меня собрано несколько точнейших фактов, для доказательства, как отец ваш, господин Бурдовский, совершенно не деловой человек, получив пятнадцать тысяч в приданое за вашею матушкой, бросил службу, вступил в коммерческие предприятия, был обманут, потерял капитал, не выдержал горя, стал пить, отчего заболел и наконец преждевременно умер, на восьмом году после брака с вашею матушкой. Затем, по собственному свидетельству матушки вашей, она осталась в нищете и совсем погибла бы без постоянной и великодушной помощи Павлищева, выдававшего ей до шестисот рублей в год вспоможения. Затем есть бесчисленные свидетельства, что вас, ребенка, он полюбил чрезвычайно. По этим свидетельствам и опять-таки по подтверждению матушки вашей выходит, что полюбил он вас потому преимущественно, что вы имели в детстве вид косноязычного, вид калеки, вид жалкого, несчастного ребенка (а у Павлищева, как я вывел по точным доказательствам, была всю жизнь какая-то особая нежная склонность ко всему угнетенному и природой обиженному, особенно в детях, — факт, по моему убеждению, чрезвычайно важный для нашего дела). Наконец, я могу похвалиться точнейшими изысканиями о том главном факте, как эта чрезвычайная привязанность к вам Павлищева (стараниями которого вы поступили в гимназию и учились под особым надзором) породила, наконец, мало-помалу, между родственниками и домашними Павлищева мысль, что вы сын его и что ваш отец был только обманутый муж. Но главное в том, что мысль эта укрепилась до точного и всеобщего убеждения только в последние годы жизни Павлищева, когда все испугались за завещание и когда первоначальные факты были забыты, а справки невозможны. Без сомнения, мысль эта дошла и до вас, господин Бурдовский, и завладела вами вполне. Ваша матушка, с которою я имел честь познакомиться лично, хоть и знала про все эти слухи, но даже и до сих пор не знает (я тоже скрыл от нее), что и вы, ее сын, находились под обаянием этого слуха. Многоуважаемую матушку вашу, господин Бурдовский, я застал в Пскове в болезнях и в самой крайней бедности, в которую впала она по смерти Павлищева. Она со слезами благодарности сообщила мне, что только чрез вас и чрез помощь вашу и живет на свете; она много ожидает от вас в будущем и горячо верит в будущие ваши успехи...

human_translations.translator_1: “Enough, Mr Terentyev, enough,” Gavrila Ardalionovich at last succeeded in getting a word in, “calm down, don’t upset yourself so. I heard you’re very ill! I sympathize with you. In that case, if you wish, I have finished. In conclusion I’ll only present you with a few brief facts, which, I’m convinced, would be of general interest,” he added, noticing that there was again a stir of impatience. “I only wish, backed by evidence, to inform all concerned parties that your mother, Mr Burdovsky, was favoured and supported by Pavlishchev, solely because she was the sister of that peasant girl with whom Nikolai Andreyevich Pavlishchev had fallen in love in his very early youth and whom he was fully intending to marry but for her untimely death. I have proof that this family matter, accurate in every respect, is so little known that it has almost been forgotten. I have further evidence that your mother as a ten-year-old girl was taken by Mr Pavlishchev into his family for her upbringing, that she had been promised a considerable dowry, and that all this munificence had engendered much unsavoury talk amongst Pavlishchev’s numerous relatives. Some even suspected that he’d marry his ward, but in the end at the age of twenty she married for love, for which I have the most unarguable proof, a clerk from the land survey department, one Mr Burdovsky. Here I can produce some incontrovertible facts to prove that this Mr Burdovsky, a highly impractical man, having come into fifteen thousand roubles of your mother’s dowry, left his employment, launched a commercial enterprise, was swindled, lost his capital and his grip on himself, took to drink, fell ill as a result and, seven years into his marriage with your mother, died suddenly. Subsequently, on your mother’s personal evidence, she was left destitute and would have perished totally but for Pavlishchev’s generous assistance, who made her an allowance of up to six hundred roubles per annum. Then there is no end of evidence that he took you, as a child, deeply to his heart. According to this evidence, and the further corroboration of your mother, it transpired that his love for you stemmed in the main from the fact that since childhood you had the woebegone, pathetic aspect of a pitiable, underdeveloped child. Now, Pavlishchev, as I was able to establish incontrovertibly, all his life long displayed a peculiar tenderness to all who were oppressed and naturally discriminated against, especially children – to my mind this is significant and highly pertinent to the matter at hand. Finally, I am proud to reveal that my enquiries yielded a most incontestable detail of how this extraordinary attachment that Pavlishchev manifested for you (thanks to which you were able to enter a high school and continue your studies under special supervision) eventually gave rise to the suspicion in Pavlishchev’s household and amongst his relatives, that you were his natural son and that your father was merely a cuckolded husband. But the important thing was that this suspicion turned into a cast-iron conviction only towards the latter days of Pavlishchev’s life, when everyone became concerned as to his last will and testament and after the initial facts were forgotten, and enquiries became impossible. Doubtless, rumour of this suspicion reached you too, Mr Burdovsky, and captured your imagination. Your mother, whom I had the honour of getting to know personally and who, though she herself was aware of this rumour, has no idea even to this day (and I was not forthcoming on this point), that you too, her son, had fallen prey to this rumour. I met your highly esteemed mother, Mr Burdovsky, in Pskov, gravely ill and subsisting in the abject poverty which overtook her following Pavlishchev’s death. She said with tears of gratitude that she owed her life to you and your assistance, and that she has high hopes in your future and believes with all her heart in your future fortune—”

human_translations.translator_4: Will nothing make you understand?" "Enough! enough! Mr. Terentieff," interrupted Gania. "Don't excite yourself; you seem very ill, and I am sorry for that. I am almost done, but there are a few facts to which I must briefly refer, as I am convinced that they ought to be clearly explained once for all… . " A movement of impatience was noticed in his audience as he resumed: "I merely wish to state, for the information of all concerned, that the reason for Mr. Pavlicheff's interest in your mother, Mr. Burdovsky, was simply that she was the sister of a serf-girl with whom he was deeply in love in his youth, and whom most certainly he would have married but for her sudden death. I have proofs that this circumstance is almost, if not quite, forgotten. I may add that when your mother was about ten years old, Pavlicheff took her under his care, gave her a good education, and later, a considerable dowry. His relations were alarmed, and feared he might go so far as to marry her, but she gave her hand to a young land-surveyor named Burdovsky when she reached the age of twenty. I can even say definitely that it was a marriage of affection. After his wedding your father gave up his occupation as land-surveyor, and with his wife's dowry of fifteen thousand roubles went in for commercial speculations. As he had had no experience, he was cheated on all sides, and took to drink in order to forget his troubles. He shortened his life by his excesses, and eight years after his marriage he died. Your mother says herself that she was left in the direst poverty, and would have died of starvation had it not been for Pavlicheff, who generously allowed her a yearly pension of six hundred roubles. Many people recall his extreme fondness for you as a little boy. Your mother confirms this, and agrees with others in thinking that he loved you the more because you were a sickly child, stammering in your speech, and almost deformed—for it is known that all his life Nicolai Andreevitch had a partiality for unfortunates of every kind, especially children. In my opinion this is most important. I may add that I discovered yet another fact, the last on which I employed my detective powers. Seeing how fond Pavlicheff was of you,—it was thanks to him you went to school, and also had the advantage of special teachers —his relations and servants grew to believe that you were his son, and that your father had been betrayed by his wife. I may point out that this idea was only accredited generally during the last years of Pavlicheff's life, when his next-of-kin were trembling about the succession, when the earlier story was quite forgotten, and when all opportunity for discovering the truth had seemingly passed away. No doubt you, Mr. Burdovsky, heard this conjecture, and did not hesitate to accept it as true. I have had the honour of making your mother's acquaintance, and I find that she knows all about these reports. What she does not know is that you, her son, should have listened to them so complaisantly. I found your respected mother at Pskoff, ill and in deep poverty, as she has been ever since the death of your benefactor. She told me with tears of gratitude how you had supported her; she expects much of you, and believes fervently in your future success… "

translation: Varvara Ardalionovna was a young woman of twenty-three, of average height, rather thin, with a face that wasn't particularly beautiful but contained a secret that it was pleasing to look at without necessarily being passionate about it. She resembled her mother quite a bit, and was almost dressed the same way as her mother due to a complete lack of desire to get dressed up. Her grey eyes could sometimes have a very lively and affectionate glint to them, but they were far more often serious and thoughtful, and sometimes even too much so, especially recently. Her firm and resolute expression was evident on her face, but it was felt that this firmness was possibly even more energetic and enterprising than her mother's. Varvara Ardalionovna was rather quick-tempered, and her little brother even sometimes feared this quick-temper. The guest sitting with them now, Ivan Petrovich Ptiitsyn, also feared it. He was a young man of about thirty, modestly but elegantly dressed, with pleasant but somehow rather too solemn manners. His dark red beard suggested he didn't have any government business. He was able to talk cleverly and interestingly, but more often he remained silent. In general, he seemed pleasant. He was clearly not indifferent to Varvara Ardalionovna and didn't hide his feelings. Varvara Ardalionovna treated him in a friendly way, but would sometimes delay answering some of his questions, even refusing to answer them; however, Ptiitsyn was far from being taken aback. Nina Alexandrovna was being kind to him, and had even begun to trust him a lot lately. It was known, however, that he specifically made a business of making money by lending their money at high interest on relatively secure collateral. With Ganin, he was a particularly dear friend.
source_text: Варвара Ардалионовна была девица лет двадцати трех, среднего роста, довольно худощавая, с лицом не то чтобы очень красивым, но заключавшим в себе тайну нравиться без красоты и до страсти привлекать к себе. Она была очень похожа на мать, даже одета была почти так же, как мать, от полного нежелания наряжаться. Взгляд ее серых глаз подчас мог быть очень весел и ласков, если бы не бывал всего чаще серьезен и задумчив, иногда слишком даже, особенно в последнее время. Твердость и решимость виднелись и в ее лице, но предчувствовалось, что твердость эта даже могла быть энергичнее и предприимчивее, чем у матери. Варвара Ардалионовна была довольно вспыльчива, и братец иногда даже побаивался этой вспыльчивости. Побаивался ее и сидевший теперь у них гость, Иван Петрович Птицын. Это был еще довольно молодой человек, лет под тридцать, скромно, но изящно одетый, с приятными, но как-то слишком уж солидными манерами. Темно-русая бородка обозначала в нем человека не с служебными занятиями. Он умел разговаривать умно и интересно, но чаще бывал молчалив. Вообще он производил впечатление даже приятное. Он был видимо неравнодушен к Варваре Ардалионовне и не скрывал своих чувств. Варвара Ардалионовна обращалась с ним дружески, но на иные вопросы его отвечать еще медлила, даже их не любила; Птицын, впрочем, далеко не был обескуражен. Нина Александровна была к нему ласкова, а в последнее время стала даже много ему доверять. Известно, впрочем, было, что он специально занимается наживанием денег отдачей их в быстрый рост под более или менее верные залоги. С Ганей он был чрезвычайным приятелем.

translation: "Don't cry, Mrs. Grubach," said K. and looked out the window, thinking only of Fräulein Bürstner and that she had taken a strange girl into her room. "Don't cry," he said again as he turned back into the room and saw that Mrs. Grubach was still crying. "It wasn't so bad back then, either, from my point of view. We simply misunderstood each other. That can happen even to old friends." Mrs. Grubach adjusted the apron under her eyes to see if K. was genuinely reconciled. "Well, it's like that," said K. and, assuming from Mrs. Grubach's behavior that the head clerk had not betrayed him, ventured to add: "Do you really think I could be hostile towards you over a strange girl?" "That's it, Mr. K.," said Mrs. Grubach, it was her misfortune that as soon as she felt the slightest bit more at ease, she would say something unbecoming. "I kept wondering to myself: Why is Mr. K. taking such an interest in Fräulein Bürstner? Why does he quarrel with me on her account, even though he knows that any harsh word from him keeps me awake at night? I said nothing but what I saw with my own eyes." K. said nothing to this; he should have dismissed her with the first word, but he didn't want to. He contented himself with drinking his coffee and letting Mrs. Grubach know she was being superfluous. Outside, one could hear the slow steps of Fräulein Montag, who was crossing the entire anteroom. "Do you hear that?" K. asked and pointed towards the door with his hand. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach and sighed, "I wanted to help her and even asked the maid to help, but she's stubborn, she wants to move everything on her own. I'm surprised by Fräulein Bürstner. It often bothers me that I have Fräulein Montag in lodgings, but Fräulein Bürstner takes her into her room." You don't have to worry about that, K. said and crushed the sugar crystals in his cup. "Are you harmed by that?" "No," said Mrs. Grubach, "it's welcome as far as I'm concerned. I get a room free and can put my nephew, the head clerk, in there. I was already worried that he might disturb you in the past few days when I had to let him stay in the living room next door. He doesn't take much consideration." "What a notion!" said K. and stood up, "there's no question of it. You seem to think I'm over-sensitive because I can't stand Fräulein Montag's wanderings – now she's going back again." Mrs. Grubach felt helpless. "Shall I tell her, Mr. K., to postpone the rest of the move? If you want, I'll do it right away." "But she should move to Fräulein Bürstner!" said K. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach, she didn't quite understand what K. meant. "Well then," said K., "she must take her things over there." Mrs. Grubach just nodded. This mute powerlessness, which outwardly looked no different from obstinacy, irritated K. even more. He began walking back and forth in the room from the window to the door, thus depriving Mrs. Grubach of the opportunity to leave, which she probably would have done otherwise.
source_text: »Weinen Sie doch nicht, Frau Grubach«, sagte K. und sah zum Fenster hinaus, er dachte nur an Fräulein Bürstner und daran, daß sie ein fremdes Mädchen in ihr Zimmer aufgenommen hatte. »Weinen Sie doch nicht«, sagte er nochmals, als er sich ins Zimmer zurückwandte und Frau Grubach noch immer weinte. »Es war ja damals auch von mir nicht so schlimm gemeint. Wir haben eben einander gegenseitig mißverstanden. Das kann auch alten Freunden einmal geschehen.« Frau Grubach rückte die Schürze unter die Augen, um zu sehen, ob K. wirklich versöhnt sei. »Nun ja, es ist so«, sagte K. und wagte nun, da, nach dem Verhalten der Frau Grubach zu schließen, der Hauptmann nichts verraten hatte, noch hinzuzufügen: »Glauben Sie denn wirklich, daß ich mich wegen eines fremden Mädchens mit Ihnen verfeinden könnte?« »Das ist es ja eben, Herr K.«, sagte Frau Grubach, es war ihr Unglück, daß sie, sobald sie sich nur irgendwie freier fühlte, gleich etwas Ungeschicktes sagte. »Ich fragte mich immerfort: Warum nimmt sich Herr K. so sehr des Fräulein Bürstner an? Warum zankt er ihretwegen mit mir, obwohl er weiß, daß mir jedes böse Wort von ihm den Schlaf nimmt? Ich habe ja über das Fräulein nichts anderes gesagt, als was ich mit eigenen Augen gesehen habe.« K. sagte dazu nichts, er hätte sie mit dem ersten Wort aus dem Zimmer jagen müssen, und das wollte er nicht. Er begnügte sich damit, den Kaffee zu trinken und Frau Grubach ihre Überflüssigkeit fühlen zu lassen. human_translations.translator_1: “Please don’t cry, Frau Grubach,” said K., gazing out the window; he was thinking only of Fräulein Bürstner and that she was taking a stranger into her room. “Please don’t cry,” he said again, as he turned back toward the room and Frau Grubach continued to weep. “I didn’t mean to be so harsh either then. We just misunderstood one another. That happens sometimes, even to old friends.” Frau Grubach lowered the apron from her eyes to see if K. was truly appeased. “That’s all it was,” said K., and ventured to add, since he gathered from Frau Grubach ’s behavior that the captain hadn’t told her anything: “Do you really think I’d let some young woman I don’t really know come between us?” “That’s just it, Herr K.,” said Frau Grubach, whose misfortune it was to say something awkward the moment she began to relax in the least, “I kept asking myself: Why is Herr K. taking such an interest in Fräulein Bürstner? Why is he arguing with me about her, when he knows I lose sleep over every angry word he says? After all, all I said about Fräulein Bürstner was what I’d seen with my own eyes.” K. made no reply; it would have meant driving her from the room at the very first word, and he didn’t want to do that. He was content to drink his coffee and allow Frau Grubach to feel superfluous. Outside, the dragging steps of Fräulein Montag could be heard once more along the entire length of the hall. “Do you hear that?” asked K., pointing toward the door. “Yes,” Frau Grubach said with a sigh, “I wanted to help her, and have the maid help too, but she’s stubborn, she wants to move everything herself. I’m surprised at Fräulein Bürstner. I regret having Fräulein Montag as a boarder often enough, and now Fräulein Bürstner is taking her into her own room.” “That shouldn’t bother you,” said K., crushing the sugary residue in his cup. “Do you lose anything by it?” “No,” said Frau Grubach, “it’s even good as far as I’m concerned; it leaves a room free for my nephew, the captain. I’ve been worried he might have bothered you the last few days while I had to let him sleep next door in the living room. He’s not particularly considerate.” “What an idea!” said K., standing up; “not in the least. You seem to think I’m overly sensitive just because I can’t stand listening to Fräulein Montag—there she goes back again—making all those trips.” Frau Grubach found herself at a loss. “Should I tell her to postpone the rest of the move, Herr K.? This silent helplessness, which had the surface appearance of stubbornness, irritated K. even further. He began pacing back and forth in the room from window to door, giving Frau Grubach no opportunity to slip away, which she would otherwise no doubt have done.

translation: "Don't cry, Mrs. Grubach," said K., and he looked out the window; he was thinking only of Fräulein Bürstner and that she had taken a strange girl into her room. "Don't cry," he said again, turning back into the room and seeing that Mrs. Grubach was still crying. "It wasn't that bad, by the way, from my side. We just misunderstood each other. That can happen even to old friends." Mrs. Grubach adjusted her apron over her eyes to see if K. was truly reconciled. "Well, that's how it is," said K. and, taking his cue from Mrs. Grubach's behavior, felt brave enough to add: "Do you really think I could become enemies with you because of a strange girl?" "That's exactly the point, Mr. K.," said Mrs. Grubach; it was her misfortune that as soon as she felt more at ease, she would always say something unfortunate. "I kept wondering: why is Mr. K. so taken with Fräulein Bürstner? Why is he quarreling with me on her account, even though he knows that a single unkind word from him takes away my sleep? I said nothing more about Fräulein Bürstner than what I've seen with my own eyes." K. said nothing; he should have thrown her out of the room with her first word, but he didn't want to. He satisfied himself with drinking his coffee and letting Mrs. Grubach feel uncomfortable. Outside, one could hear the plodding step of Fräulein Montag as she traversed the entire anteroom. "Do you hear that?" K. asked and pointed with his hand towards the door. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach and sighed, "I wanted to help and have the maid help, but she's obstinate, she wants to do everything herself. I'm surprised at Fräulein Bürstner. It's often annoying that I have Fräulein Montag as a tenant, but Fräulein Bürstner even takes her into her room." You don't have to worry about that, K. said, and crushed the sugar residue in the cup. "Do you have any loss from it?" "No," said Mrs. Grubach, "actually, I find it perfectly all right; I get a room free and can put my nephew, the Captain, there. I was already worried that he might have disturbed you in the last few days, when I had to keep him in the living room next door; he doesn't take much notice." "What a notion!" said K. and stood up, "that's not even in question. You seem to think me over-sensitive because I can't stand Fräulein Montag's comings and goings – now she's going back – at all." Mrs. Grubach felt rather helpless. "Should I, Mr. K., tell her to put off the rest of the move? If you want, I'll do it right away." "But she should move to Fräulein Bürstner!" said K. source_text: »Weinen Sie doch nicht, Frau Grubach«, sagte K. und sah zum Fenster hinaus, er dachte nur an Fräulein Bürstner und daran, daß sie ein fremdes Mädchen in ihr Zimmer aufgenommen hatte. »Weinen Sie doch nicht«, sagte er nochmals, als er sich ins Zimmer zurückwandte und Frau Grubach noch immer weinte. »Es war ja damals auch von mir nicht so schlimm gemeint. Wir haben eben einander gegenseitig mißverstanden. Das kann auch alten Freunden einmal geschehen.« Frau Grubach rückte die Schürze unter die Augen, um zu sehen, ob K. wirklich versöhnt sei. »Nun ja, es ist so«, sagte K. und wagte nun, da, nach dem Verhalten der Frau Grubach zu schließen, der Hauptmann nichts verraten hatte, noch hinzuzufügen: »Glauben Sie denn wirklich, daß ich mich wegen eines fremden Mädchens mit Ihnen verfeinden könnte?« »Das ist es ja eben, Herr K.«, sagte Frau Grubach, es war ihr Unglück, daß sie, sobald sie sich nur irgendwie freier fühlte, gleich etwas Ungeschicktes sagte. »Ich fragte mich immerfort: Warum nimmt sich Herr K. so sehr des Fräulein Bürstner an? Warum zankt er ihretwegen mit mir, obwohl er weiß, daß mir jedes böse Wort von ihm den Schlaf nimmt? Ich habe ja über das Fräulein nichts anderes gesagt, als was ich mit eigenen Augen gesehen habe.« K. sagte dazu nichts, er hätte sie mit dem ersten Wort aus dem Zimmer jagen müssen, und das wollte er nicht. Er begnügte sich damit, den Kaffee zu trinken und Frau Grubach ihre Überflüssigkeit fühlen zu lassen. Draußen hörte man wieder den schleppenden Schritt des Fräulein Montag, welche das ganze Vorzimmer durchquerte. »Hören Sie es?« fragte K. und zeigte mit der Hand nach der Tür. »Ja«, sagte Frau Grubach und seufzte, »ich wollte ihr helfen und auch vom Dienstmädchen helfen lassen, aber sie ist eigensinnig, sie will alles selbst übersiedeln. Ich wundere mich über Fräulein Bürstner. Mir ist es oft lästig, daß ich Fräulein Montag in Miete habe, Fräulein Bürstner aber nimmt sie sogar zu sich ins Zimmer.« Das muß Sie gar nicht kümmern, sagte K. und zerdrückte die Zuckerreste in der Tasse. »Haben Sie denn dadurch einen Schaden?« »Nein«, sagte Frau Grubach, »an und für sich ist es mir ganz willkommen, ich bekomme dadurch ein Zimmer frei und kann dort meinen Neffen, den Hauptmann, unterbringen. Ich fürchtete schon längst, daß er Sie in den letzten Tagen, während derer ich ihn nebenan im Wohnzimmer wohnen lassen mußte, gestört haben könnte. Er nimmt nicht viel Rücksicht.« »Was für Einfälle!« sagte K. und stand auf, »davon ist ja keine Rede. Sie scheinen mich wohl für überempfindlich zu halten, weil ich diese Wanderungen des Fräulein Montag – jetzt geht sie wieder zurück – nicht vertragen kann.« Frau Grubach kam sich recht machtlos vor. »Soll ich, Herr K., sagen, daß sie den restlichen Teil der Übersiedelung aufschieben soll? Wenn Sie wollen, tue ich es sofort.« »Aber sie soll doch zu Fräulein Bürstner übersiedeln!« sagte K. »Ja«, sagte Frau Grubach, sie verstand nicht ganz, was K. meinte. »Nun also«, sagte K., »dann muß sie doch ihre Sachen hinübertragen.« Frau Grubach nickte nur. Diese stumme Hilflosigkeit, die äußerlich nicht anders aussah als Trotz, reizte K. noch mehr. Er fing an, im Zimmer vom Fenster zur Tür auf und ab zu gehen und nahm dadurch Frau Grubach die Möglichkeit, sich zu entfernen, was sie sonst wahrscheinlich getan hätte.

translation:
"Do cry, Mrs. Grubach," said K. and looked out the window. He was only thinking about Fräulein Bürstner and that she had taken a strange girl into her room. "Do cry," he said again as he turned back into the room and saw that Mrs. Grubach was still crying. "It wasn't meant to be so serious at the time," he said. "We just misunderstood each other, that's all. Such misunderstandings can happen even between old friends." Mrs. Grubach pushed back the apron to see if K. really was reconciled. "Well, yes, that's how it is," said K. and, judging from Mrs. Grubach's behavior, dared to add, as long as she hadn't betrayed the Captain yet, "Do you really think I could become hostile towards you because of a strange girl?" "That's exactly it, Mr. K.," said Mrs. Grubach, for her misfortune was that, as soon as she felt a bit freer, she would say something awkward right away. "I was always wondering, Mr. K., why you're so taken with Fräulein Bürstner, why you argue with me on her account, although you know that every harsh word from you keeps me awake. I said nothing but what I had seen with my own eyes."

K. said nothing to this; he should have thrown her out of the room with the first word, but he didn't want to do that. He just drank his coffee and let Mrs. Grubach know that she was being superfluous. Outside, one could hear the slow steps of Fräulein Montag again, who was crossing the entire entry hall. "Do you hear that?" he asked and pointed with his hand towards the door. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach and sighed, "I wanted to help her and also have the maid help, but she's stubborn, she wants to do everything herself. I wonder about Fräulein Bürstner; it's often a nuisance that I have Fräulein Montag as a tenant, but Fräulein Bürstner takes her in to her room."

That doesn't have to concern you, said K. and crushed the sugar lumps in his cup. "Do you suffer any loss from it?" "No," said Mrs. Grubach, "it's quite welcome to me, as a matter of fact, for I get a room free and can house my nephew, the Captain, there. I was already worried that he might have disturbed you in the last few days, when I had to let him stay next door in the living room. He doesn't take much notice of others."

"What fancy notions!" said K. and stood up, "there's no point in talking about that. You must think me rather sensitive because I can't stand Fräulein Montag's wanderings – now she's going back – anymore." Mrs. Grubach felt rather helpless. "Should I, Mr. K., tell her to postpone the rest of the move? If you want, I'll do it right away." "But she's supposed to move in with Fräulein Bürstner!" said K. "Yes," said Mrs. Grubach, she didn't quite understand what K. meant. "Well then," said K., "she'll have to move her belongings over there." Mrs. Grubach just nodded. This mute helplessness, which looked just as obstinate from the outside, only ticked K. off even more. He started pacing back and forth in the room from the window to the door, thus depriving Mrs. Grubach of the chance to leave, which she probably would have taken otherwise.
source_text: »Weinen Sie doch nicht, Frau Grubach«, sagte K. und sah zum Fenster hinaus, er dachte nur an Fräulein Bürstner und daran, daß sie ein fremdes Mädchen in ihr Zimmer aufgenommen hatte. »Weinen Sie doch nicht«, sagte er nochmals, als er sich ins Zimmer zurückwandte und Frau Grubach noch immer weinte. »Es war ja damals auch von mir nicht so schlimm gemeint. Wir haben eben einander gegenseitig mißverstanden. Das kann auch alten Freunden einmal geschehen.« Frau Grubach rückte die Schürze unter die Augen, um zu sehen, ob K. wirklich versöhnt sei. »Nun ja, es ist so«, sagte K. und wagte nun, da, nach dem Verhalten der Frau Grubach zu schließen, der Hauptmann nichts verraten hatte, noch hinzuzufügen: »Glauben Sie denn wirklich, daß ich mich wegen eines fremden Mädchens mit Ihnen verfeinden könnte?« »Das ist es ja eben, Herr K.«, sagte Frau Grubach, es war ihr Unglück, daß sie, sobald sie sich nur irgendwie freier fühlte, gleich etwas Ungeschicktes sagte. »Ich fragte mich immerfort: Warum nimmt sich Herr K. so sehr des Fräulein Bürstner an? Warum zankt er ihretwegen mit mir, obwohl er weiß, daß mir jedes böse Wort von ihm den Schlaf nimmt? Ich habe ja über das Fräulein nichts anderes gesagt, als was ich mit eigenen Augen gesehen habe.« K. sagte dazu nichts, er hätte sie mit dem ersten Wort aus dem Zimmer jagen müssen, und das wollte er nicht. Er begnügte sich damit, den Kaffee zu trinken und Frau Grubach ihre Überflüssigkeit fühlen zu lassen. Draußen hörte man wieder den schleppenden Schritt des Fräulein Montag, welche das ganze Vorzimmer durchquerte. »Hören Sie es?« fragte K. und zeigte mit der Hand nach der Tür. »Ja«, sagte Frau Grubach und seufzte, »ich wollte ihr helfen und auch vom Dienstmädchen helfen lassen, aber sie ist eigensinnig, sie will alles selbst übersiedeln. Ich wundere mich über Fräulein Bürstner. Mir ist es oft lästig, daß ich Fräulein Montag in Miete habe, Fräulein Bürstner aber nimmt sie sogar zu sich ins Zimmer.« Das muß Sie gar nicht kümmern, sagte K. und zerdrückte die Zuckerreste in der Tasse. »Haben Sie denn dadurch einen Schaden?« »Nein«, sagte Frau Grubach, »an und für sich ist es mir ganz willkommen, ich bekomme dadurch ein Zimmer frei und kann dort meinen Neffen, den Hauptmann, unterbringen. Ich fürchtete schon längst, daß er Sie in den letzten Tagen, während derer ich ihn nebenan im Wohnzimmer wohnen lassen mußte, gestört haben könnte. Er nimmt nicht viel Rücksicht.« »Was für Einfälle!« sagte K. und stand auf, »davon ist ja keine Rede. Sie scheinen mich wohl für überempfindlich zu halten, weil ich diese Wanderungen des Fräulein Montag – jetzt geht sie wieder zurück – nicht vertragen kann.« Frau Grubach kam sich recht machtlos vor. »Soll ich, Herr K., sagen, daß sie den restlichen Teil der Übersiedelung aufschieben soll? Wenn Sie wollen, tue ich es sofort.« »Aber sie soll doch zu Fräulein Bürstner übersiedeln!« sagte K. »Ja«, sagte Frau Grubach, sie verstand nicht ganz, was K. meinte. »Nun also«, sagte K., »dann muß sie doch ihre Sachen hinübertragen.« Frau Grubach nickte nur. Diese stumme Hilflosigkeit, die äußerlich nicht anders aussah als Trotz, reizte K. noch mehr. Er fing an, im Zimmer vom Fenster zur Tür auf und ab zu gehen und nahm dadurch Frau Grubach die Möglichkeit, sich zu entfernen, was sie sonst wahrscheinlich getan hätte.

"I always wondered to myself: why is Mr. K. taking such an interest in Fräulein Bürstner? Why is he quarreling with me because of her, when he knows that any harsh word from him takes away my sleep? I said nothing but what I saw with my own eyes about Fräulein Bürstner." K. didn't say anything, he should have thrown her out with her first word, but he didn't want to. He limited himself to drinking his coffee and letting Frau Grubach feel uncomfortable. Outside one could hear the slow steps of Fräulein Montag, who walked through the entire anteroom. "Do you hear it?" K. asked and gestured with his hand towards the door. "Yes," said Frau Grubach, and sighed, "I wanted to help her, and also have the maid help, but she is obstinate, she wants to move everything herself. I'm surprised by Fräulein Bürstner. It often annoys me that I have Fräulein Montag in rent, but Fräulein Bürstner even takes her in to her room." You don't have to concern yourself with that, said K. and crushed the sugar remnants in his cup. "Are you harmed by it?" "No," said Frau Grubach, "in itself it's fine with me, I get a room free that way and can move my nephew, the Hauptmann, in there. I was already worried that he could bother you in the last days, while I had to put him up in the next room. He takes little consideration." "What absurd ideas!" said K. and stood up, "there's no talk of that. You seem to think me over-sensitive because I can't stand Fräulein Montag's wanderings – now she's going back again." Frau Grubach felt quite helpless. "Should I, Mr. K., tell her to delay the rest of the move? If you want, I'll do it right away." "But she should move to Fräulein Bürstner!" said K. source_text: »Weinen Sie doch nicht, Frau Grubach«, sagte K. und sah zum Fenster hinaus, er dachte nur an Fräulein Bürstner und daran, daß sie ein fremdes Mädchen in ihr Zimmer aufgenommen hatte. »Weinen Sie doch nicht«, sagte er nochmals, als er sich ins Zimmer zurückwandte und Frau Grubach noch immer weinte. »Es war ja damals auch von mir nicht so schlimm gemeint. Wir haben eben einander gegenseitig mißverstanden. Das kann auch alten Freunden einmal geschehen.« Frau Grubach rückte die Schürze unter die Augen, um zu sehen, ob K. wirklich versöhnt sei. »Nun ja, es ist so«, sagte K. und wagte nun, da, nach dem Verhalten der Frau Grubach zu schließen, der Hauptmann nichts verraten hatte, noch hinzuzufügen: »Glauben Sie denn wirklich, daß ich mich wegen eines fremden Mädchens mit Ihnen verfeinden könnte?« »Das ist es ja eben, Herr K.«, sagte Frau Grubach, es war ihr Unglück, daß sie, sobald sie sich nur irgendwie freier fühlte, gleich etwas Ungeschicktes sagte. »Ich fragte mich immerfort: Warum nimmt sich Herr K. so sehr des Fräulein Bürstner an? Warum zankt er ihretwegen mit mir, obwohl er weiß, daß mir jedes böse Wort von ihm den Schlaf nimmt? Ich habe ja über das Fräulein nichts anderes gesagt, als was ich mit eigenen Augen gesehen habe.« K. sagte dazu nichts, er hätte sie mit dem ersten Wort aus dem Zimmer jagen müssen, und das wollte er nicht. Er begnügte sich damit, den Kaffee zu trinken und Frau Grubach ihre Überflüssigkeit fühlen zu lassen. Draußen hörte man wieder den schleppenden Schritt des Fräulein Montag, welche das ganze Vorzimmer durchquerte. »Hören Sie es?« fragte K. und zeigte mit der Hand nach der Tür. »Ja«, sagte Frau Grubach und seufzte, »ich wollte ihr helfen und auch vom Dienstmädchen helfen lassen, aber sie ist eigensinnig, sie will alles selbst übersiedeln. Ich wundere mich über Fräulein Bürstner. Mir ist es oft lästig, daß ich Fräulein Montag in Miete habe, Fräulein Bürstner aber nimmt sie sogar zu sich ins Zimmer.« Das muß Sie gar nicht kümmern, sagte K. und zerdrückte die Zuckerreste in der Tasse. »Haben Sie denn dadurch einen Schaden?« »Nein«, sagte Frau Grubach, »an und für sich ist es mir ganz willkommen, ich bekomme dadurch ein Zimmer frei und kann dort meinen Neffen, den Hauptmann, unterbringen. Ich fürchtete schon längst, daß er Sie in den letzten Tagen, während derer ich ihn nebenan im Wohnzimmer wohnen lassen mußte, gestört haben könnte. Er nimmt nicht viel Rücksicht.« »Was für Einfälle!« sagte K. und stand auf, »davon ist ja keine Rede. Sie scheinen mich wohl für überempfindlich zu halten, weil ich diese Wanderungen des Fräulein Montag – jetzt geht sie wieder zurück – nicht vertragen kann.« Frau Grubach kam sich recht machtlos vor. »Soll ich, Herr K., sagen, daß sie den restlichen Teil der Übersiedelung aufschieben soll? Wenn Sie wollen, tue ich es sofort.« »Aber sie soll doch zu Fräulein Bürstner übersiedeln!« sagte K. »Ja«, sagte Frau Grubach, sie verstand nicht ganz, was K. meinte. »Nun also«, sagte K., »dann muß sie doch ihre Sachen hinübertragen.« Frau Grubach nickte nur. Diese stumme Hilflosigkeit, die äußerlich nicht anders aussah als Trotz, reizte K. noch mehr. Er fing an, im Zimmer vom Fenster zur Tür auf und ab zu gehen und nahm dadurch Frau Grubach die Möglichkeit, sich zu entfernen, was sie sonst wahrscheinlich getan hätte.

translation:
Just as they were drinking and celebrating, someone came to report: "Great King, there are two horned ghost kings outside who want to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let them in." The ghost king rushed in, prostrating himself on the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What business do you have with me?" The ghost king replied, "I have long heard that the Great King is recruiting the wise and the capable, and I have never had the chance to see him. Today I see the Great King granting the heavenly script, and I have achieved success and renown. I especially came to present this vermilion cloak to the Great King, to congratulate him on his good fortune. I, a lowly one, dare not be rejected; I would be grateful if you would accept me, and I would be willing to serve you like a dog or a horse."

The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the vermilion cloak. All the others were delighted and lined up in order to pay their respects to the Monkey King. The Monkey King then appointed the ghost king as the commander-in-chief of the vanguard. The ghost king finished his thanks and said, "Great King, you have been in heaven for a long time, what position have you been given?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor favors the wise and has appointed me to be something called a 'Bamboo Warden'!" The ghost king heard this and then said, "Great King, you have such magical powers, why would you be responsible for taking care of horses? Why not just be a 'Pacifier of Heaven' and see no harm in it?" The Monkey King heard this and was extremely pleased, saying "Good! Good! Good!" and ordered his four mighty generals: "Quickly, set up a banner with the four characters 'Pacifier of Heaven' on it, and raise it up high. From now on, only refer to me as the Pacifier of Heaven, and do not call me Great King again. Also, inform all the other goblin kings in the various caves of this change."
source_text: 正饮酒欢会间，有人来报道：“大王，门外有两个独角鬼王，要见大王。”猴王道：“教他进来。”那鬼王整衣跑入洞中，倒身下拜。美猴王问他：“你见我何干？”鬼王道：“久闻大王招贤，无由得见；今见大王授了天录，得意荣归，特献赭黄袍一件，与大王称庆。肯不弃鄙贱，收纳小人，亦得效犬马之劳。”猴王大喜，将赭黄袍穿起，众等欣然排班朝拜，即将鬼王封为前部总督先锋。鬼王谢恩毕，复启道：“大王在天许久，所授何职？”猴王道：“玉帝轻贤，封我做个甚么‘弼马温’！”鬼王听言，又奏道：“大王有此神通，如何与他养马？就做个‘齐天大圣’，有何不可？”猴王闻说，欢喜不胜，连道几个“好！好！好！”教四健将：“就替我快置个旌旗，旗上写‘齐天大圣’四大字，立竿张挂。自此以后，只称我为齐天大圣，不许再称大王。亦可传与各洞妖王，一体知悉。”此不在话下。

The Monkey King said, "Teach him to come in." The Monkey King asked him, "Why do you see me?" The Ghost King said, "I've heard for a long time that the King is recruiting talents, but I can't see it; now I see the King conferring the Tianlu, and he is proud to return, and he specially presents a ochre and yellow robe to be called by the King. Celebration. Willing to not abandon the contemptible, accepting the villain, and also the labor of the dog and horse." The Monkey King was overjoyed, put on the ochre and yellow robe, and all the others were happy to arrange their shifts to worship, and the Ghost King was named the pioneer of the former governor. The Ghost King thanked him and said again, "Your Majesty has been in the sky for a long time, what position has he granted him?" The Monkey King said, "The Jade Emperor Qingxian, make me a 'Bi Ma Wen'!" The Ghost King heard the words and said again: " The king has such supernatural powers, how to raise horses with him? Just be a 'Great Sage Equalling the Sky', why not?" The Monkey King heard that, overjoyed, and repeated several times, "Good! Good! Good!" "Just set up a flag for me, write the four characters of 'Monkey King' on the flag, and hang it on the pole. From then on, I will only be called the Monkey King, not the king. It can also be passed on to the other cave demons. King, I know all of them." That's not a problem.

human_translations.translator_1: As they were drinking wine and conversing happily, someone came to report: “ Great King, there are two one-horned demon kings outside who want to see you.” “Show them in,” said the Monkey King. The demon kings straightened out their attire, ran into the cave, and prostrated themselves. “Why did you want to see me?” asked the Handsome Monkey King. “We have long heard that the Great King is receptive to talents,” said the demon kings, “but we had no reason to request your audience. Now we learn that our Great King has received a divine appointment and has returned in success and glory. We have come, therefore, to present the Great King with a red and yellow robe for his celebration. If you are not disdainful of the uncouth and the lowly and are willing to receive us plebeians, we shall serve you as dogs or as horses.” Highly pleased, the Monkey King put on the red and yellow robe while the rest of them lined up joyfully and did homage. He then appointed the demon kings to be the Vanguard Commanders, Marshals of the Forward Regiments. After expressing their thanks, the demon kings asked again, “Since our Great King was in Heaven for a long time, may we ask what kind of appointment he received?” “The Jade Emperor belittles the talented,” said the Monkey King. “He only made me something called the BanHorsePlague.” Hearing this, the demon kings said again, “Great King has such divine powers! Why should you take care of horses for him? What is there to stop you from assuming the rank of the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven?” When the Monkey King heard these words, he could not conceal his delight, shouting repeatedly, “Bravo! Bravo!” “Make me a banner immediately,” he ordered the four mighty commanders, “and inscribe on it in large letters, ‘The Great Sage, Equal to Heaven.’ Erect a pole to hang it on. From now on, address me only as the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven, and the title Great King will no longer be permitted. translation:
As they were drinking and feasting together, someone came to report, "The Great King, there are two horned kings of ghosts at the door, asking to see the Great King." The Monkey King said, "Let them come in." The horned king came in, hurriedly removing his coat and bowing to the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What brings you here to see me?" The horned king replied, "I have long heard that the Great King is recruiting talent and haven't had the chance to meet him. Today, having been granted the Heavenly Classic, I've returned in triumph and come to offer a piece of cinnabar-colored robes as a gift, to celebrate with the Great King. Would you deign to take in a humble man, and allow me to render my services like a dog or a horse?"

The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the cinnabar-colored robes. The assembly stood in line and bowed respectfully to pay their homage. Thereupon, the Monkey King promoted the horned king to the position of Commander-in-Chief and Vanguard. The horned king expressed his gratitude, and then asked, "Great King, it's been a long time since You've been in heaven, what position were You given?" The Monkey King replied, "The Jade Emperor has slighted You and gave me the title of 'Protector of Horses'!" The horned king then said, "With Your supernatural abilities, how could You possibly tend horses? Why not be called 'The Grand Sage Who Extends Heaven' instead?" The Monkey King was overjoyed and repeatedly exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! Excellent!" He instructed his four mighty generals, "Hurry up and set up a pennant with the four words 'Grand Sage Who Extends Heaven' written on it. From now on, everyone shall address me as the Grand Sage Who Extends Heaven, and not call me Great King again. You may also inform the other kings of the various caves of this new title, so that they'll all be aware of it."

human_translations.translator_1: As they were drinking wine and conversing happily, someone came to report: “ Great King, there are two one-horned demon kings outside who want to see you.” “Show them in,” said the Monkey King. The demon kings straightened out their attire, ran into the cave, and prostrated themselves. “Why did you want to see me?” asked the Handsome Monkey King. “We have long heard that the Great King is receptive to talents,” said the demon kings, “but we had no reason to request your audience. Now we learn that our Great King has received a divine appointment and has returned in success and glory. We have come, therefore, to present the Great King with a red and yellow robe for his celebration. If you are not disdainful of the uncouth and the lowly and are willing to receive us plebeians, we shall serve you as dogs or as horses.” Highly pleased, the Monkey King put on the red and yellow robe while the rest of them lined up joyfully and did homage. He then appointed the demon kings to be the Vanguard Commanders, Marshals of the Forward Regiments. After expressing their thanks, the demon kings asked again, “Since our Great King was in Heaven for a long time, may we ask what kind of appointment he received?” “The Jade Emperor belittles the talented,” said the Monkey King. “He only made me something called the BanHorsePlague.” Hearing this, the demon kings said again, “Great King has such divine powers! From now on, address me only as the Great Sage, Equal to Heaven, and the title Great King will no longer be permitted. The Monster Kings of the various caves will also be informed so that it will be known to all.” Of this we shall speak no further.
human_translations.translator_2: Whilst they were drinking wine together, there came in a man, who said, “Great King, at our gate there are two one horned kings, who wish to see you.” The Monkey King said, “Let them come in.” The two kings outside straightened their clothes, entered the cave, kowtowed and said, “We have long heard of the Great King who is in search of worthy officials, but we had no opportunity of meeting him before. Now we have heard that the Great King has been given a post in heaven. He must be pleased, and have come back with honors. So we have come to present him with a yellow robe as a token of congratulation. If he will kindly accept it, please let him use it as he does his horses and dogs.” The Monkey King was very pleased, put on the yellow robe and appointed the demon kings as viceroys under him. Having thanked him for his favor, the demon kings said, “You were in heaven a long time, what rank did you occupy there?” The Monkey King replied, “The Jade Emperor did not respect me, and simply appointed me to look after some horses.” The demon kings said, “Since you, Great King, have marvelous magic powers, how did you submit to merely looking after horses? If you had called yourself the Great Sage, the Equal of Heaven, there would have been nothing you could not have done.” The Monkey King was delighted beyond measure on hearing this, and could not refrain from repeating, “Good, Good, Good!” several times. He ordered his four generals to make him a banner on which was to be written in large letters, “The Great Sage, the Equal of Heaven.” He put up a tall flagstaff and hoisted the banner, and cried, “Henceforth never again call me the Great King, but the Great Sage, the Equal of Heaven. Report this to all the demon chiefs, so that they may know.” The day after the Monkey King had left his post in heaven, when the court was about to assemble, the Master of Ceremonies brought in the two assistant grooms instead of the Horse Master. They knelt before the throne and said, “We beg to say that the new Horse Master, not satisfied with the low position assigned to him, has left Heaven altogether.”
human_translations.translator_3: In the middle of the banquet, two visitors were announced: a pair of rhinoceros-horned demon kings. As soon as Monkey had them shown in, they rushed up to prostrate themselves. “Having heard about your Heavenly appointment and that you’d returned covered in glory, we wish to congratulate you with this red and yellow robe and to offer our faithful service.” Monkey happily slipped on the robe, accepted the adulation of the entire banqueting hall, and appointed the demon kings his frontline commanders. “Just as a matter of interest, what post did Heaven give you?” the new arrivals asked. “That crummy Jade Emperor made me his groom,” grumbled Monkey. “What?” The demon kings seemed astonished. “How could an omnipotent magic monkey be made to look after horses? You are the Great Sage Equal to Heaven!” Monkey thought this was the best thing ever. “Quick as you can,” he ordered his generals, “make me a flag saying ‘The Great Sage Equal to Heaven’ and mount it on a bamboo pole. No more of this ‘Great King’ rubbish. And tell my brothers the monstrous monarchs, too.” * * * • • •
human_translations.translator_4: As they were drinking someone came in to report, “Your Majesty, there are two Single-horned Devil Kings outside who want to see you.” “Ask them in,” said the Monkey King, and the two formally-dressed devil kings hurried into the cave and prostrated themselves. “Why have you come to see me?” asked the Handsome Monkey King; and they replied, “We have long heard that Your Majesty is looking for men of talent, but we were unable to see you before. The Monkey King said, "Invite them in." The devil king straightened his clothes and rushed into the cave, prostrating himself on the ground. The Monkey King asked him, "What business do you have with me?" The devil king replied, "For a long time I have heard that the Great King attracts talents, yet I have never had the chance to see you; today I see that you have been granted the heavenly scripture and returned to glory, so I've come to present you with a piece of vermilion garb as a congratulatory gift. Would you deign to accept a lowly subject and bestow upon me a position to serve you, allowing me to discharge my humble duties as a loyal servant." The Monkey King was overjoyed and put on the vermilion robe. The assembly praised and respectfully lined up to pay homage, and the Monkey King promoted the devil king to the position of Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief of the vanguard. The devil king thanked him and then said, "The Great King has been in heaven for a long time; what office has he been given?" The devil king heard this and suggested, "The Great King has such divine abilities; how could he bother with attending horses? Let's just call him the 'Universal Sage' instead, what's wrong with that?" The Monkey King heard this and was overjoyed, repeating several times, "Good! Good! Good!" Let the news be passed on to all the devil kings in the various caves."

translation: A call from the next room startled him so that he slammed his teeth against the glass. "The warden is calling for you," it said. It was only the screaming that startled him, that short, abrupt, military screaming that he wouldn't have suspected from the warden Franz. The command itself was very welcome. "At last!" he exclaimed, locked the wardrobe and immediately hastened into the next room. There the two warders were waiting and herded him, as if it were only natural, back into his room. "What are you doing?" they shouted. "You want to appear in your undergarments before the warden? He will thrash you and us too!" "Leave me alone, the devil!" K. cried, already being pushed back to his wardrobe. "If you overpower me in bed, don't expect to find me in a dinner jacket!" "It's pointless," said the warders, who became as calm, almost melancholic, whenever K. shouted, thereby confusing or, as it were, bringing him to his senses. "Absurd ceremonies!" he muttered, but was already picking up a coat from the chair and holding it for a moment in both hands, as if offering it to the judgment of the warders. They shook their heads. "It has to be a black coat," they said. K. then threw the coat to the ground and said – he didn't know what sense he meant by it –: "It's not the main hearing yet." The warders smiled, but stuck to their: "It has to be a black coat." "If I hasten the matter by doing so, let it be so," said K., opened the wardrobe himself, searched among the many clothes for a long time, chose his best black outfit, a jacket coat that had caused a stir among his acquaintances almost because of its tailoring, and now also pulled out another shirt and began to dress with care. In secret, he believed he had achieved a speeding up of the whole affair by making the warders forget to force him to take a bath. He watched them to see if they might still remember, but of course they didn't, whereas Willem did not forget to send Franz to inform the warden that K. was getting dressed.
source_text: Da erschreckte ihn ein Zuruf aus dem Nebenzimmer derartig, daß er mit den Zähnen ans Glas schlug. »Der Aufseher ruft Sie!« hieß es. Es war nur das Schreien, das ihn erschreckte, dieses kurze, abgehackte, militärische Schreien, das er dem Wächter Franz gar nicht zugetraut hätte. Der Befehl selbst war ihm sehr willkommen. »Endlich!« rief er zurück, versperrte den Wandschrank und eilte sofort ins Nebenzimmer. Dort standen die zwei Wächter und jagten ihn, als wäre das selbstverständlich, wieder in sein Zimmer zurück. »Was fällt Euch ein?« riefen sie. »Im Hemd wollt Ihr vor den Aufseher? Er läßt Euch durchprügeln und uns mit!« »Laßt mich, zum Teufel!« rief K., der schon bis zu seinem Kleiderkasten zurückgedrängt war, »wenn man mich im Bett überfällt, kann man nicht erwarten, mich im Festanzug zu finden.« »Es hilft nichts«, sagten die Wächter, die immer, wenn K. schrie, ganz ruhig, ja fast traurig wurden und ihn dadurch verwirrten oder gewissermaßen zur Besinnung brachten. »Lächerliche Zeremonien!« brummte er noch, hob aber schon einen Rock vom Stuhl und hielt ihn ein Weilchen mit beiden Händen, als unterbreite er ihn dem Urteil der Wächter. Sie schüttelten die Köpfe. »Es muß ein schwarzer Rock sein«, sagten sie. K. warf daraufhin den Rock zu Boden und sagte – er wußte selbst nicht, in welchem Sinne er es sagte –: »Es ist doch noch nicht die Hauptverhandlung.« Die Wächter lächelten, blieben aber bei ihrem: »Es muß ein schwarzer Rock sein.« »Wenn ich dadurch die Sache beschleunige, soll es mir recht sein«, sagte K., öffnete selbst den Kleiderkasten, suchte lange unter den vielen Kleidern, wählte sein bestes schwarzes Kleid, ein Jackettkleid, das durch seine Taille unter den Bekannten fast Aufsehen gemacht hatte, zog nun auch ein anderes Hemd hervor und begann, sich sorgfältig anzuziehen. Im geheimen glaubte er, eine Beschleunigung des Ganzen damit erreicht zu haben, daß die Wächter vergessen hatten, ihn zum Bad zu zwingen. Er beobachtete sie, ob sie sich vielleicht daran doch erinnern würden, aber das fiel ihnen natürlich gar nicht ein, dagegen vergaß Willem nicht, Franz mit der Meldung, daß sich K. anziehe, zum Aufseher zu schicken.

translation: As he was startled by a call from the neighboring room, he hit his teeth on the glass. "The supervisor is calling you!" it said. It was just the screaming that startled him, this brief, clipped, military screaming, which Franz the warden would never have expected of him. The order itself was very welcome. "Finally!" he shouted back, locked the wardrobe and hurried immediately into the neighboring room. There the two wardens chased him back to his room as if it was self-evident. "What's gotten into you?" they shouted. "You want to appear in a shirt before the supervisor? He'll let you get beaten and us off with it!" "Leave me alone, to the devil with it!" K. shouted, who was already pushed back to his closet. "If you attack me in bed, you can't expect to find me in a dinner jacket!" "It's all for nothing," said the wardens, who always became completely calm, yes, almost sad when K. shouted, and thus confused or rather brought to his senses him. "Absurd ceremonies!" he grumbled, but already lifted a jacket from the chair and held it for a moment with both hands, as if he were offering it to the judgment of the wardens. They shook their heads. "It must be a black suit," they said. K. then threw the jacket on the floor and said – he did not even know in what sense he said it –: "It's not even the main hearing yet." The wardens smiled, but stuck to their: "It must be a black suit." "If I hasten the matter this way, it's all right with me," said K., opened the closet himself, searched for a long time among the many clothes, selected his best black clothes, a jacket coat that had caused almost a sensation among his acquaintances because of its tailoring, now also pulled out another shirt and began to dress carefully. In secret, he believed he had achieved a speed-up of the whole process by making the wardens forget to force him to bathe. He observed them, whether they might still remember, but of course they didn't forget to do that, but Willem did not forget to report to Franz that K. was getting dressed to send him to the supervisor.

Der Befehl selbst war ihm sehr willkommen. »Endlich!« rief er zurück, versperrte den Wandschrank und eilte sofort ins Nebenzimmer. translation: It was a call from the adjacent room that frightened him so that he banged his teeth against the glass. "The overseer is calling you!" it said. It was just the shouting that frightened him, that short, staccato, military shouting, which he wouldn't have attributed to the guard Franz. The order itself was very welcome. "At last!" he called back, locked the wardrobe and immediately hurried into the adjacent room. There, the two guards were waiting for him and chased him back into his room as if it was the most natural thing. "What are you doing?" they shouted. "You want to go before the overseer in your underwear? He'll thrash you and us too!" "Leave me be, the devil!" cried K., who was already being pushed back to his wardrobe. "If someone attacks you in bed, you can't expect to be found in your formal attire." "It's no use," said the guards, who, whenever K. shouted, became entirely calm, yes almost sad, and thus confused or, in a way, brought to their senses. "Ridiculous formalities!" he grumbled, but already lifted a coat from the chair and held it for a moment with both hands, as if he were presenting it to the judgment of the guards. They shook their heads. "It must be a black coat," they said. K. then threw the coat to the floor and said – he didn't know in what sense he said it – "It's not the main trial yet." The guards smiled, but stuck to their: "It must be a black coat." "If I speed things up this way, it's all right with me," said K., opened the wardrobe himself, searched for a long time among the many clothes, chose his best black outfit, a jacket-coat that had already drawn attention among his acquaintances due to its cut, and now pulled out another shirt as well, and began to dress carefully. In secret, he believed he had achieved a speeding up of the whole affair by making the guards forget to force him to take a bath. He observed them, whether they might remember it anyway, but that didn't occur to them, whereas Willem didn't forget to send Franz with the message to tell the overseer that K. was getting dressed.

Thereupon K. flung the coat on the floor and said -- he did not himself know in what sense he meant the words -- " But this isn't the capital charge yet." The warders smiled, but stuck to their: "It must be a black coat." "If it's to dispatch my case any quicker, I don't mind," replied K., opening the wardrobe, where he searched for a long time among his many suits, chose his best black one, a lounge suit which had caused almost a sensation among his acquaintances because of its elegance, then selected another shirt and began to dress with great care. In his secret heart he thought he had managed after all to speed up the proceedings, for the warders had forgotten to make him take a bath. He kept an eye on them to see if they would remember the ducking, but of course it never occurred to them, yet on the other hand Willem did not forget to send Franz to the Inspector with the information that K. was dressing.

translation: Crossing himself according to Russian custom, he set to work. Under the guise of selecting a place to live and with various pretexts, he set about glancing at one region and another of our state, and above all those that had suffered most from unfortunate events, crop failures, deaths, and other calamities - in short, wherever it would be possible to buy the necessary people at a convenient and cheap price. He did not knock on the door of any landowner at random, but chose people to his liking or those with whom he could make such deals with the least difficulty, first making sure to get acquainted with them, winning them over to himself, in order to, if possible, acquire the peasants through friendship rather than purchase. So, readers should not be indignant with the author if the people he has introduced do not meet with their approval; it is Chichikov's fault, he is the full master here, and we should follow him wherever he pleases. From our side, if we indeed incur blame for the paleness and lack of definition of the characters' faces and personalities, let us just say that one does not see the full scope of the matter at the beginning. The arrival in any city, even the capital, is always somewhat pale; at first everything is dull and monotonous: the endless factories and factories stretch out, choked with smoke, and then the angles of six-story houses, shops, billboards, enormous city vistas, all decorated with belfries, columns, statues, towers, with the city's brilliance, noise, and thunder, and all the wonders that the hand and mind of man have produced. As the first purchases were seen by the reader; how the story will proceed, what successes and failures the hero will have, how he will overcome the more difficult obstacles, how the colossal images will appear, and the hidden levers of the broad narrative will be moved, and the distant horizon of the story will ring out, and it will take on a majestic, lyrical flow, then he will see it later. There is still a long way to go for the traveling carriage consisting of a middle-aged gentleman, a bercy in which bachelors ride, a servant Pyotr, a coachman Selifan, and three horses, known from the Assessor to the lustful underling. And so, here is our hero as he is. But perhaps some readers will demand a final definition in one sentence: is he relative to moral qualities? He is not a hero, full of virtues and virtues, this is obvious. So who is he? He must be a scoundrel? Why is he a scoundrel, and why should he be so strict with others? Now, we do not have scoundrels, there are people who are well-intentioned, pleasant, and such as to publicly expose their physiognomy to a slap in the face for universal shame, can be found only two, three people, and even they now speak of virtues. It is fairest to call him: the owner, the acquirer. Acquisitions - are the basis of everything; from them arose the affairs, which the light of day does not give a very clean name. True, in such a character there is already something repulsive, and the same reader, who on his life's path will be friends with such a person, will conduct him with bread and salt and have a good time with him, but he will look askance at him if he finds himself in the hero of a drama or an epic. He is wise who is not disgusted by any character, but, gazing at it in a scrutinizing way, unravels it to its original causes. All of a sudden, everything turns into a man; you can't even turn around before a terrible worm, who has taken control of all the life juices, has grown inside him. And not only is it a great passion, but even a slight passion for something small can grow into something born for great deeds, causing him to forget great and sacred duties and see great and sacred things in insignificant trinkets. Countless as the sands on the seashore are human passions, and all are different from one another, and all, base and beautiful, are first submissive to man, and then become his terrifying rulers. Blessed is he who has chosen the most beautiful passion from all; it grows and multiplies with each hour and minute without measure, and he enters deeper and deeper into the boundless heaven of his soul. But there are passions whose choice is not up to man. They were born with him in the moment of his birth into the world, and he is not given the strength to resist them. They are guided by higher characteristics, and in them there is something eternal, unceasing, throughout his life. The earthly great path is destined for them to achieve: all the same, in a dark or radiant appearance, or radiating joy, gladdening the world - equally, they are summoned by an unknown man for the unknown good. And maybe, in this very Chichikov, the passion drawing him is not from him, and in his cold existence lies that which will later cast him to the dust and to the knees before the heavenly wisdom. And there is a mystery why this image has appeared in the present poem.
source_text: Перекрестясь по русскому обычаю, приступил он к исполнению. Под видом избрания места для жительства и под другими предлогами предпринял он заглянуть в те и другие углы нашего государства, и преимущественно в те, которые более других пострадали от несчастных случаев, неурожаев, смертностей и прочего и прочего, — словом, где бы можно удобнее и дешевле накупить потребного народа. Он не обращался наобум ко всякому помещику, но избирал людей более по своему вкусу или таких, с которыми бы можно было с меньшими затруднениями делать подобные сделки, стараясь прежде познакомиться, расположить к себе, чтобы, если можно, более дружбою, а не покупкою приобрести мужиков. Итак, читатели не должны негодовать на автора, если лица, доныне являвшиеся, не пришлись по его вкусу; это вина Чичикова, здесь он полный хозяин, и куда ему вздумается, туда и мы должны тащиться. С нашей стороны, если, точно, падет обвинение за бледность и невзрачность лиц и характеров, скажем только то, что никогда вначале не видно всего широкого теченья и объема дела. Въезд в какой бы ни было город, хоть даже в столицу, всегда как-то бледен; сначала все серо и однообразно: тянутся бесконечные заводы да фабрики, закопченные дымом, а потом уже выглянут углы шестиэтажных домов, магазины, вывески, громадные перспективы улиц, все в колокольнях, колоннах, статуях, башнях, с городским блеском, шумом и громом и всем, что на диво произвела рука и мысль человека. Как произвелись первые покупки, читатель уже видел; как пойдет дело далее, какие будут удачи и неудачи герою, как придется разрешить и преодолеть ему более трудные препятствия, как предстанут колоссальные образы, как двигнутся сокровенные рычаги широкой повести, раздастся далече ее горизонт и вся она примет величавое лирическое течение, то увидит потом. Еще много пути предстоит совершить всему походному экипажу, состоящему из господина средних лет, брички, в которой ездят холостяки, лакея Петрушки, кучера Селифана и тройки коней, уже известных поименно от Заседателя до подлеца чубарого. Итак, вот весь налицо герой наш, каков он есть! Но потребуют, может быть, заключительного определения одною чертою: кто же он относительно качеств нравственных? Что он не герой, исполненный совершенств и добродетелей, это видно. Кто же он? стало быть, подлец? Почему ж подлец, зачем же быть так строгу к другим? Теперь у нас подлецов не бывает, есть люди благонамеренные, приятные, а таких, которые бы на всеобщий позор выставили свою физиогномию под публичную оплеуху, отыщется разве каких-нибудь два, три человека, да и те уже говорят теперь о добродетели. Справедливее всего назвать его: хозяин, приобретатель. Приобретение — вина всего; из-за него произвелись дела, которым свет дает название не очень чистых. Правда, в таком характере есть уже что-то отталкивающее, и тот же читатель, который на жизненной своей дороге будет дружен с таким человеком, будет водить с ним хлеб-соль и проводить приятно время, станет глядеть на него косо, если он очутится героем драмы или поэмы. Но мудр тот, кто не гнушается никаким характером, но, вперя в него испытующий взгляд, изведывает его до первоначальных причин. Быстро все превращается в человеке; не успеешь оглянуться, как уже вырос внутри страшный червь, самовластно обративший к себе все жизненные соки. И не раз не только широкая страсть, но ничтожная страстишка к чему-нибудь мелкому разрасталась в рожденном на лучшие подвиги, заставляла его позабывать великие и святые обязанности и в ничтожных побрякушках видеть великое и святое. Бесчисленны, как морские пески, человеческие страсти, и все не похожи одна на другую, и все они, низкие и прекрасные, вначале покорны человеку и потом уже становятся страшными властелинами его. Блажен избравший себе из всех прекраснейшую страсть; растет и десятерится с каждым часом и минутой безмерное его блаженство, и входит он глубже и глубже в бесконечный рай своей души. Но есть страсти, которых избранье не от человека. Уже родились они с ним в минуту рожденья его в свет, и не дано ему сил отклониться от них. Высшими начертаньями они ведутся, и есть в них что-то вечно зовущее, неумолкающее во всю жизнь. Земное великое поприще суждено совершить им: все равно, в мрачном ли образе, или пронестись светлым явленьем, возрадующим мир, — одинаково вызваны они для неведомого человеком блага. И, может быть, в сем же самом Чичикове страсть, его влекущая, уже не от него, и в холодном его существовании заключено то, что потом повергнет в прах и на колени человека пред мудростью небес. И еще тайна, почему сей образ предстал в ныне являющейся на свет поэме.
