translation: — No?! No!!! Rognin screamed, on the verge of frenzy with joy, — no?! And they told me... Ah! Nastasya Filippovna! They say you've agreed to marry Ganya! With him?! Can that be?! (I've told them all!). Why, I'd buy him off for a hundred roubles, I'll give him a thousand, no, three, just to back out, and he flees on the eve of the wedding, leaving me the bride. Why, Ganya, scoundrel! Why didn't he take three thousand?! There you go, that's what they're after; he was traveling all the way to get you to sign such a bond; he said: 'I'll buy you' and he'll buy you!
source_text: — Нет? Нет!! — вскричал Рогожин, приходя чуть не в исступление от радости, — так нет же?! А мне сказали они... Ах! Ну!.. Настасья Филипповна! Они говорят, что вы помолвились с Ганькой! С ним-то? Да разве это можно? (Я им всем говорю!). Да я его всего за сто рублей куплю, дам ему тысячу, ну, три, чтоб отступился, так он накануне свадьбы бежит, а невесту всю мне оставит. Ведь так, Ганька, подлец! Ведь уж взял бы три тысячи! Вот они, вот! С тем и ехал, чтобы с тебя подписку такую взять; сказал: куплю — и куплю!
gt_translation: - Not? Not!! exclaimed Rogozhin, going almost into a frenzy with joy, “isn’t it?! And they told me... Ah! Well!... Nastasya Filippovna! They say you got engaged to Ganka! With him? Is it possible? (I tell them all!). Yes, I’ll buy him for just a hundred rubles, I’ll give him a thousand, well, three, so that he backs down, so he runs away on the eve of the wedding, and leaves the whole bride to me. It's true, Ganka, you scoundrel! After all, I would have taken three thousand! Here they are, here they are! With that I went to take such a subscription from you; said: I will buy - and I will buy!

human_translations.translator_1: “Really? Really?” Rogozhin exclaimed in an ecstasy of joy. “Is that so?! And I was told… My word! Well I never!… Nastasya Filippovna! They told me you’d got engaged to that there Ganya! What, to him? I couldn’t believe it! I said so at once! translation: The venerable Xuanzang was fated to be here at this moment. Like a Lo Han from the Blissful Realm, he surpassed the wonderful achievements of those in the Western Land of True Enlightenment. He carried a staff that resonated with nine cymbals and a monastic hat that glimmered with profuse adornments. Truly, this was a genuine transmission of the Buddha's teachings, surpassing even the flawless wisdom of Bodhi. At the time, all scholars and officials cheered, and Emperor Taizong was overjoyed. He then vested the venerable Xuanzang in a monk's robes and handed him a sacred staff. The emperor also gifted him two teams of attendants and assigned many officials to escort him out of the palace gates and instruct him to go to the temple. He walked on the main street as if he was a proud participant in a special examination, receiving prestigious titles. Xuanzang repeatedly bowed to express his gratitude. On the street, the enthusiastic cheers and applause shook the air. Everyone in Chang'an City, whether merchants, traders, sons of nobles, scholars, or literary figures, big men and small women alike, all vied to watch and praise him, saying in unison, "This is a wonderful master! He is indeed a living embodiment of a Lo Han descending to the world, a bodhisattva come among mortals." Xuanzang proceeded to the temple, where monks came to welcome him. When they saw him wearing his monk's robes and carrying his staff, they said, "The Guardian King of the Underworld has come!" They all gathered around him in reverence and service. Xuanzang ascended to the hall, burned incense to pay homage to the Buddha, and then expressed his gratitude to the emperor before the assembly, after which they all returned to their meditation seats. Unbeknownst to him, the sun had set, casting a reddish glow to the west. It was just the moment when the capital's drum and bell were just starting to ring out, marking the end of the day's business. The staff's gongs silenced the people's footsteps. Above, the temples were ablaze with candles, while the countryside lay deserted and quiet. The monks were engrossed in meditation, immersed in scriptures, and perfecting their inner nature.

translation:
The Great Master Xuanzang was most fortunate to have arrived at the right moment to accept this office. He looked just like a Bodhisattva from the Saha World, surpassing the blessed ones from the Western regions. His staff clinking with nine rings, his Bhikkhu hat reflecting numerous jade designs. This was truly a faithful transmission of the Buddha's lineage, surpassing even the unwavering wisdom of Bodhi. At that moment, the literati and martial classes all cheered in front of him, the Emperor himself was overjoyed beyond words, and thus bestowed upon the Master a monk's robes and a precious staff, and two teams of attendants to escort him out of the palace gates, instructing him to walk on the street and proceed to the temple. It was as if the valedictorian of the imperial examination was being honored in a grand procession.

The Great Master Xuanzang bowed in gratitude once more, and as he walked through the street, the road was filled with commotion and excitement, like the swaying and bustling of a festival. You see, in the Longan city, the merchants, business owners, nobles and sons of nobles, poets and scholars, the young and the old, all hurried to look and praise him, saying in unison: "This is a true and living Arhat come down to the mortal world, a living Bodhisattva descended to the human realm."

The Great Master Xuanzang walked to the temple, where monks came out to welcome him. As soon as they saw him wearing this monk's robes and carrying this staff, they exclaimed that the Heaven King of the Great Treasure had come, and all of them bowed in reverence, serving him left and right. The Great Master Xuanzang ascended the hall, incense burning, offering incense to the Buddha, and then addressed the assembly, expressing his gratitude to the sacred teachings. After finishing his words, they all returned to their meditation seats. Meanwhile, the sun was setting, with mist shrouding the grass and trees, and the Imperial City's drum struck its first beat, announcing nightfall. The sound of the three beats ceased, the palace was quiet, the front and rear courtyards were still. The temple lights were shining bright, a village in the distance was dark and quiet. The monks were immersed in meditation, while the scripture lessons continued.

The monk Xuanzang was incredibly fortunate, to be born with the karma to receive this honor. He shone like a saint in the realm of Bliss, surpassing the virtues of the Bodhisattva of the West. With his staff striking the ground with a resounding nine-hued sound, his Pusapata hat reflected the depths of his wisdom. This was truly the embodiment of the son of the Buddha, not a mere rumor or hearsay. The emperor himself was overjoyed, and ordered him to don the monastic robes and take the staff of the Dharma. He also assigned two teams of attendants to escort him, and many officials accompanied him as he walked out of the palace gates, instructing him to proceed to the temple as if he were the number one scholar holding high honors. 

Xuanzang bowed to express his gratitude, and in the midst of the bustling street, people shook and rustled with excitement. Look at the city of Chang'an, merchants and merchants, princes and nobles, scholars and men of letters, young and old, all rushed to catch a glimpse and praise him, saying in unison: "What a remarkable monk! He is indeed a living Arhat, descending to the mortal realm, a living Bodhisattva, incarnate in the world." 

Xuanzang continued on to the temple, where the monks came out to welcome him, greeting him as if the Lord of the Underworld himself had arrived. They were all overjoyed, venerating him from left and right. After ascending the temple steps, Xuanzang lit incense, bowed to the Buddha, and gave thanks to the benevolence of the emperor. Having finished his devotions, he returned to his seat. Suddenly, as dusk set in, with the smoke of the setting sun shrouding the grass and the imperial drums beginning to ring out, the three strokes of the temple gong stopped people in their tracks, bringing a stillness to the palace grounds. Up in the temple, the bright lights of the lanterns shone forth, but the distant village fell silent and dark. The monks were in a state of deep meditation, and were thoroughly devoted to the study and contemplation of the scriptures.

translation: But speaking of Tripitaka accompanying Monkey King on their westward journey, after travelling for several days, it was the cold season in the month of Lá (approximately January), the biting wind was howling, the snow was freezing, and they were traversing a rugged road amidst steep cliffs, perilous peaks, and rugged mountains. Tripitaka was sitting on his horse, and at a distance he heard the sound of rushing water resonating in his ears. He turned around and called, "Monkey, where's the sound of water coming from?" Monkey replied, "I remember this place is called Snake Ridge Mountain Eagles' Sorrow Gorge, and it's probably the sound of water coming from the gorge." No sooner had he said this than the horse arrived at the edge of the gorge. Tripitaka pulled on the reins to look, but all he saw was: the pulse of the water flowing like frost, the crystal clear waves reflecting the red sun. The sound of the night rain resonated in the secluded valley, the rainbow of dawn shone in the vast sky. The thousand-fathom high waves rose and splashed like jade, the waters tumbling and roaring made the wind clear. The currents flowed back into the smoke and misty waters, the egrets and herons forgot their forgotten fishing spots. Just as the master and disciple were gazing at the scene, a resounding noise came from the centre of the gorge, and a dragon suddenly emerged, stirring up the waves and crashing against the mountainside. It pounced at Tripitaka. Monkey was startled and lost his luggage, and hastily took his master down from the horse and turned to run back. The dragon gave chase, but couldn't catch up. It swallowed his white horse whole, and then hid underwater. Monkey brought his master to a high precipice and sat him down, then came back to retrieve his luggage, but only found one bundle of luggage left behind. He took the bundle of luggage and carried it to his master, saying, "Master, that wicked dragon has vanished into thin air, but it has scared off my horse." Tripitaka asked, "Disciple, how are you going to find your horse?" Monkey replied, "Don't worry, don't worry. Let me go and take a look."

Relax!” said Pilgrim. “Let me go and have a look!”
human_translations.translator_2: ON THE PILGRIMS WENT, till they came to the Golden Temple where Shakyamuni had once preached. There they were hospitably received by the abbot, who said grace before eating. Attached to the temple was an orphanage. There they met a monk 105 years old, who told them, privately, that the king’s daughter was in the orphanage. She declared she had been carried off and placed in this temple by the demons, whilst a witch had been substituted as the royal princess in the palace. He begged them to find out the truth of this, as every night the true princess begged him to help her. The pilgrims promised to do what they could. On entering the city in search of the king’s palace, to get his passport signed, the Master and Sun found a strange ceremony taking place. The king’s only daughter had fixed on that very day and hour to throw a colored silk ball on the head of her chosen husband. She threw it at the Master, and carried him to the palace, amid the congratulations of all the people. But the Master said he was on an important mission, and must consult his three disciples, as to what was to be done. He was warned that if he did not accept the princess’ choice he would he killed. This threw the Master into a great fear and he waited anxiously for the appearance of his disciples, for whom he had sent. The three disciples were invited to the royal palace. On entering the royal presence, the three stood upright, and none of them knelt.
human_translations.translator_3: Chapter Nineteen After a series of remarkable events—Pigsy falling into the Buddha’s honey-trap; a piqued Monkey demolishing a holy tree laden with magical fruits resembling newborn babies; Pigsy, Tripitaka, and Sandy being lacquered; and Monkey being fried by the outraged keeper of the tree—the team of disciples made peace with the immortal horticulturalist in question, restored themselves with plenty of ginseng and cinnabar, and set off once more for the west. Soon they came to another tall mountain. “The way ahead is steep and treacherous,” observed Tripitaka, “I fear the horse will slip. Take care, all of you.” “Don’t worry, Master!” cheered Monkey. Our hero led the way, opening a path onto a high ridge. Before them lay yet another mountain range running with streams, tigers, wolves, deer, foxes, rabbits, and a thousand-foot python and a one-hundred-thousand-foot hydra, both of whom busily belched horrendous miasma. Just as Tripitaka was beginning to whimper, Monkey waved his staff and all the wild beasts scattered like so many rodents. Onward they journeyed to the summit, at which moment Tripitaka chose to say: “I’ve not had anything to eat all day. Go and beg me some food.” “Did you walk up here with your eyes shut?” Monkey responded affably. “This mountain is completely uninhabited. Even if we had money to spend, there’d be no one to sell us food.” Tripitaka now turned petulant. “Are you forgetting who rescued you from that stone casket beneath the Mountain of Two Frontiers? You owe me, Monkey! Get me something to eat before this pestilential mountain finishes me off.”
human_translations.translator_4: Monkey looked after the Tang Priest as they headed West. They had been travelling for several days in the twelfth month of the year, with its freezing North winds and biting cold. Their path wound along overhanging precipices and steep cliffs, and they crossed range after range of dangerous mountains. One day Sanzang heard the sound of water as he rode along, and he turned around to shout, “Monkey, where's that sound of water coming from?” “As I remember, this place is called Eagle's Sorrow Gorge in the Coiled Snake Mountain. It must be the water in the gorge.” Before he had finished speaking, the horse reached the edge of the gorge. Sanzang reined in and looked. He saw: A thin cold stream piercing the clouds, Deep, clear waves shining red in the sun. The sound shakes the night rain and is heard in the quiet valley, Its color throws up a morning haze that obscures the sky. A thousand fathoms of flying waves spit jade; The torrent's roar howls in the fresh wind. The current leads to the misty waves of the sea; The egret and the cormorant never meet by a fisherman. As master and disciple watched they heard a noise in the gorge as a dragon emerged from the waves, leapt up the cliff, and grabbed at Sanzang. In his alarm Monkey dropped the luggage, lifted Sanzang off his horse, turned, and fled. The dragon, unable to catch him up, swallowed the white horse, saddle and all, at a single gulp, then disappeared once more beneath the surface of the water. Monkey made his master sit down on a high peak and went back to fetch the horse and the luggage. When he found that the horse had gone and only the luggage was left, he carried the luggage up to his master and put it down before him. “Master,” he said, “that damned dragon has disappeared without a trace. It gave our horse such a fright that it ran away.” “However are we going to find the horse, disciple?” “Don't worry, don't worry, wait here while I go and look for it.”

translation: But it was said that the Monkey King attended the Tang Monk as he journeyed west, and after travelling for a few days, it was the cold season of December, with a biting north wind howling and frost and snow falling. The terrain was rugged, with towering cliffs, precipitous peaks, and towering mountains. The Master was riding his horse when he heard in the distance the sound of rushing water, like a cacophony in his ear. He turned around and called out, "Monkey, where is the sound of water coming from?" The Monkey said, "I remember that this place is called Snake Coil Mountain Hawk's Chorus Brook, and I suppose the sound is coming from the brook below." He had hardly finished speaking when the horse reached the edge of the brook. The Master pulled on the reins to look, and when he did, he saw that the water was flowing rapidly, like a cold current cutting through the clouds, its clear ripples shining in the sunlight like a rosy dawn. The sound was like the distant patter of rain on a secluded valley, the morning clouds shining brightly in the sky. The waves were foaming and crashing against the rocks, as if they were a thousand cataracts breaking against jade. A wave had crashed over and was lost in the depths, its voice echoing like a thunderous cry in the wind. The water flowed back, disappearing into the vast expanse of misty waves, where herons and cormorants seemed to have lost sight of each other in their quest for fish. Just then, the Master and his disciple happened to be watching, when a mighty roar echoed through the brook, and a dragon burst out from the middle of it, stirring up the waves and crashing against the mountain peaks. It was chasing the Master, who panicked and dropped his luggage. He jumped off the horse and rushed to his side, and then the two of them hastily ran away. The dragon gave chase, but it could not catch up to them. In its haste, it swallowed the Master's white horse, including the saddle and reins, whole, and then disappeared into the water, leaving behind no trace. The Monkey led the Master to a high platform, where he sat down, and then went back to collect the luggage and the abandoned horse, except for one load, which was nowhere to be found. He carried the luggage to the Master and said, "Master, that calamitous dragon has vanished, but it has scared my horse away." The Master asked, "Disciple, how do you plan to find the horse?" The Monkey said, "Don't worry, don't worry, let me go take a look."

The biting northerly winds howled fiercely, the frost bit, and the icy winds howled through the mountains. They were traveling on a road with overhanging cliffs, rugged ledges, precipitous mountain passes, and alternating ridges. On horseback, Tripitaka looked back and heard the rushing water's tumultuous sound. He called out, "Monkey, where is the water coming from?" Monkey replied, "I remember this place was called Snake Slithering Hill and Falcon's Lament Gully. It must be the water sound coming from the gully." Not a moment later, their horse arrived at the gully's edge, and Tripitaka pulled on the reins to stop and look, but saw only: a slender thread of icy water ran through the clouds, and a gentle wave reflected the crimson glow of dawn. The sounds of nocturnal raindrops echoed through the secluded valley; and the rippling colors of the morning sunrise dazzled the limitless sky. Waves rose a thousand fathoms and foamed and splashed against jade stones; one great wave crashed and boomed in the clear wind. The flowing water gradually returned, disappearing into the countless expanse of the haze, and the cormorants and herons forgot their fishing net. The two monks looked on in awe, just as a resounding noise came from within the gully. He brought the luggage over to his master's presence and said, "Master, the evil dragon's whereabouts are nowhere to be seen; it just scared my horse away." human_translations.translator_4: Monkey looked after the Tang Priest as they headed West. They had been travelling for several days in the twelfth month of the year, with its freezing North winds and biting cold. Their path wound along overhanging precipices and steep cliffs, and they crossed range after range of dangerous mountains. One day Sanzang heard the sound of water as he rode along, and he turned around to shout, “Monkey, where's that sound of water coming from?” “As I remember, this place is called Eagle's Sorrow Gorge in the Coiled Snake Mountain. The sound shakes the night rain and is heard in the quiet valley, Its color throws up a morning haze that obscures the sky. A thousand fathoms of flying waves spit jade; The torrent's roar howls in the fresh wind. The current leads to the misty waves of the sea; The egret and the cormorant never meet by a fisherman. As master and disciple watched they heard a noise in the gorge as a dragon emerged from the waves, leapt up the cliff, and grabbed at Sanzang. In his alarm Monkey dropped the luggage, lifted Sanzang off his horse, turned, and fled. The dragon, unable to catch him up, swallowed the white horse, saddle and all, at a single gulp, then disappeared once more beneath the surface of the water. Monkey made his master sit down on a high peak and went back to fetch the horse and the luggage. translation: As it happened, the Tang Monk was accompanied by the Monkey King westward, and they had journeyed for a few days. It was in the depths of the cold winter month, when the north wind howled fiercely and the frost was biting, and they had to traverse a mountain path which was steep and rugged, with craggy precipices and towering peaks. The Tang Monk was riding a horse, when he suddenly heard a loud rumbling sound in the distance and called out, "Monkey, where's the water roaring?" The Monkey replied, "I remember this place was called Snake Coil Mountain where the Song of the Pines resounds. It must be the sound of water flowing through the gully." He hadn't even finished speaking when the horse approached the edge of the gully, and the Tang Monk pulled on the reins to take a closer look. To his surprise, he saw a crystal clear brook that flowed through the clouds and reflected the red hues of the rising sun; the night rain-like sound of the water resonated through the secluded valley, where a riot of colors danced amidst the morning mist, filling the boundless expanse. The torrent surged and splashed, spewing out a thousand-foot-high waves that shattered into fragments like jade; one great wave crashed and roared, sending a gust of clear wind. The waters receded, returning to the countless acres of serene ripples on the horizon, and the cormorants and egrets forgot their fishing and merged into the backdrop of the scene. Just then, the two master and disciple stood transfixed, when suddenly a loud rumbling sound came from the gully, and a dragon shot out from its depths, causing the waters to churn and the waves to churn. The dragon leaped out of the precipice and down the mountain, straight towards the Tang Monk. In a state of panic, the Monkey discarded his luggage and dismounted to lift his master onto his feet, and then he turned to flee. The dragon gave chase, but failed to catch the Monkey, who then swallowed his white horse, saddle and bridle, all at once. The dragon vanished into the water, leaving no trace. The Monkey helped his master up to a high promontory and sat him down, then came back to pick up his luggage and the remaining load, but the horse was nowhere to be seen. He carried his master to the mountain's edge and presented himself before the Tang Monk, saying, "Master, that devilish dragon has vanished into thin air, and it's only taken my horse." The Tang Monk asked, "Disciple, how are you going to find the horse?" The Monkey replied, "Don't worry, don't worry, I'll go take a look."

translation: While Tripitaka was accompanying Monkey on his westward journey, the days passed, and it was now the dead of winter, with a harsh north wind blowing fiercely and ice forming thickly. The road they were traveling was fraught with steep cliffs, rugged rocks, and treacherous mountains that made one's heart skip a beat. As Tripitaka rode his horse, he could hear a distant rushing sound of water growing louder by the second, and he turned around to ask, "Monkey, where is the sound of the water?" Monkey replied, "I remember that this place is called the Serpent-helix Mountain, where a river runs. I think the sound of the water must be coming from the river." No sooner had he spoken than the horse reached the riverbank, and Tripitaka reined in his horse to look down into the river. And there, beneath the clear sky, he saw the icy water flowing swiftly, its clear ripples reflecting the red glow of the rising sun. The water's roar was like a distant thunderstorm in a hidden valley; its foamy waves seemed to be dancing with colors that were as radiant as the dawn. A thousand fathoms high, the waves rose and crashed, sending shards of jade flying; the waters roared like a clear gale, echoing through the valleys. As the waters returned to the misty pools, the herons and egrets were oblivious to the fishing that lay scattered nearby. Tripitaka and his disciple stood there in awe, watching as a mighty roar burst forth from the depths of the river, and a dragon emerged from the water's edge, sending waves crashing and buffeting the mountainside. The dragon shot out, sprang at the old monk, and frightened Monkey. In the confusion, Monkey lost his pack, leapt down from his horse to grab Tripitaka, and then fled in haste. The dragon chased after them but was unable to catch up. As it vanished into the depths of the river, it swallowed Monkey's white horse whole, leaving behind only the empty saddle and harness. Monkey returned to the old monk, who sat on a high elevation, and carried his pack to him, leaving behind only a pack without any horse. Monkey presented the pack to Tripitaka and said, "Master, the evil dragon has vanished without a trace, but it has frightened my horse away." Tripitaka asked, "My son, how shall we find the horse?" Monkey replied, "Don't worry, don't worry. Let me go take a look."

human_translations.translator_3: Chapter Nineteen After a series of remarkable events—Pigsy falling into the Buddha’s honey-trap; a piqued Monkey demolishing a holy tree laden with magical fruits resembling newborn babies; Pigsy, Tripitaka, and Sandy being lacquered; and Monkey being fried by the outraged keeper of the tree—the team of disciples made peace with the immortal horticulturalist in question, restored themselves with plenty of ginseng and cinnabar, and set off once more for the west. Soon they came to another tall mountain. “The way ahead is steep and treacherous,” observed Tripitaka, “I fear the horse will slip. Take care, all of you.” “Don’t worry, Master!” cheered Monkey. Our hero led the way, opening a path onto a high ridge. Before them lay yet another mountain range running with streams, tigers, wolves, deer, foxes, rabbits, and a thousand-foot python and a one-hundred-thousand-foot hydra, both of whom busily belched horrendous miasma. Just as Tripitaka was beginning to whimper, Monkey waved his staff and all the wild beasts scattered like so many rodents. Onward they journeyed to the summit, at which moment Tripitaka chose to say: “I’ve not had anything to eat all day. Go and beg me some food.” “Did you walk up here with your eyes shut?” Monkey responded affably. “This mountain is completely uninhabited. Even if we had money to spend, there’d be no one to sell us food.” Tripitaka now turned petulant. “Are you forgetting who rescued you from that stone casket beneath the Mountain of Two Frontiers? You owe me, Monkey! Get me something to eat before this pestilential mountain finishes me off.”
human_translations.translator_4: Monkey looked after the Tang Priest as they headed West. They had been travelling for several days in the twelfth month of the year, with its freezing North winds and biting cold. Their path wound along overhanging precipices and steep cliffs, and they crossed range after range of dangerous mountains. One day Sanzang heard the sound of water as he rode along, and he turned around to shout, “Monkey, where's that sound of water coming from?” “As I remember, this place is called Eagle's Sorrow Gorge in the Coiled Snake Mountain. It must be the water in the gorge.” Before he had finished speaking, the horse reached the edge of the gorge. Sanzang reined in and looked. He saw: A thin cold stream piercing the clouds, Deep, clear waves shining red in the sun. The sound shakes the night rain and is heard in the quiet valley, Its color throws up a morning haze that obscures the sky. A thousand fathoms of flying waves spit jade; The torrent's roar howls in the fresh wind. The current leads to the misty waves of the sea; The egret and the cormorant never meet by a fisherman. As master and disciple watched they heard a noise in the gorge as a dragon emerged from the waves, leapt up the cliff, and grabbed at Sanzang. In his alarm Monkey dropped the luggage, lifted Sanzang off his horse, turned, and fled. The dragon, unable to catch him up, swallowed the white horse, saddle and all, at a single gulp, then disappeared once more beneath the surface of the water. Monkey made his master sit down on a high peak and went back to fetch the horse and the luggage. When he found that the horse had gone and only the luggage was left, he carried the luggage up to his master and put it down before him. “Master,” he said, “that damned dragon has disappeared without a trace. It gave our horse such a fright that it ran away.” “However are we going to find the horse, disciple?” “Don't worry, don't worry, wait here while I go and look for it.”

translation: But as he sat in his stiff armchair, his mind tormented by thoughts and sleeplessness, regaling Nosdrayev and his whole family with tales, and before him a sizzling candle lit the dusty, dark shade that had long since settled over the lamp, threatening to sputter out with every passing moment, and gazing in at the dark, blind windows a night that was already beginning to pale in anticipation of the approaching dawn, and in the distance the muted sounds of distant roosters could be heard, and in a completely slumbering city, perhaps some forgotten army uniform was being sewn in a far-off seamstress's shop, a distressed soul of some unknown class and dignity, who knew only one road, far too worn down by the Russian rabble – in that same city, at the opposite end, an event was unfolding that would make our hero's position even more difficult. Indeed, in the distant streets and alleyways of the city, a very peculiar carriage creaked, arousing wonder about its name. It was not at all like a cart, a carriage, or a buggy, and was more like a thick-skinned, rounded gourd placed on wheels. The cheeks of this gourd, or rather the doors bearing the signs of yellow paint, swung badly because of the poor state of the handles and locks, which were tied together with rope. The gourd was filled with quilted pillowcases in the shape of bags, rolls, and simply pillows, stuffed with bags of bread, kalach, kukurolks, scorvolks, and sweet doughnuts, and the cream pie and rye roll poked out even above the top. The text on the wheels was occupied by a valet of a certain lineage, in a coat of homespun wool, with an unshaven beard and a light downy stubble, known by the name "the small one". The noise and shriek of the iron hinges and rusty bolts awakened a baker at the other end of the city, who, grasping his alabaster, bellowed drowsily, "Who's coming?" – but, seeing that no one was coming, and all that could be heard was the creaking far off, caught himself by the collar of some sort of beast and, approaching the lantern, executed it on the spot right on his nail. After which, putting down his alabaster, he fell asleep once again in accordance with the standards of his knighthood. The horses constantly fell on their front legs because they were not shod, and it was also clear that the deceased city pavement was unfamiliar to them. The gig, making a few turns from street to street, finally turned into a dark alleyway past a small church of Nicholas on Nedomotchki and stopped in front of the gates of the proto-priest's house. A girl emerged from the gig, wearing a headscarf and a telogreika, and slammed the gates with both fists so strongly that even a man (the small one in the homespun woolen coat had already been dragged out by the legs, as he was fast asleep) would have been knocked out. The dogs barked, and the gates finally, with great effort, swallowed this clumsy vehicle. The carriage drove into a narrow courtyard piled high with firewood, chicken coops, and various cages; a baroness emerged from the carriage: this baroness was the landowner's secretary, Korobochka. Soon after our hero's departure, a considerable worry arose regarding the possibility of his deceit, such that, not having slept for three nights in a row, she decided to travel to the city, despite the fact that the horses were not shod, and there to find out, for certain, at what price souls were being sold, and perhaps she had not erred, God forbid, in selling them at three times the price. What consequence this arrival produced, the reader will learn from a conversation between two women. But let that conversation take place in the next chapter.
source_text: Но в продолжение того, как он сидел в жестких своих креслах, тревожимый мыслями и бессонницей, угощая усердно Ноздрева и всю родню его, и перед ним теплилась сальная свечка, которой светильня давно уже накрылась нагоревшею черною шапкою, ежеминутно грозя погаснуть, и глядела ему в окна слепая, темная ночь, готовая посинеть от приближавшегося рассвета, и пересвистывались вдали отдаленные петухи, и в совершенно заснувшем городе, может быть, плелась где-нибудь фризовая шинель, горемыка неизвестно какого класса и чина, знающая одну только (увы!) слишком протертую русским забубенным народом дорогу, — в это время на другом конце города происходило событие, которое готовилось увеличить неприятность положения нашего героя. Именно, в отдаленных улицах и закоулках города дребезжал весьма странный экипаж, наводивший недоумение насчет своего названия. Он не был похож ни на тарантас, ни на коляску, ни на бричку, а был скорее похож на толстощекий выпуклый арбуз, поставленный на колеса. Щеки этого арбуза, то есть дверцы, носившие следы желтой краски, затворялись очень плохо по причине плохого состояния ручек и замков, кое-как связанных веревками. Арбуз был наполнен ситцевыми подушками в виде кисетов, валиков и просто подушек, напичкан мешками с хлебами, калачами, кокурками, скородумками и кренделями из заварного теста. Пирог-курник и пирог-рассольник выглядывали даже наверх. Запятки были заняты лицом лакейского происхожденья, в куртке из домашней пеструшки, с небритой бородою, подернутою легкой проседью, — лицо, известное под именем «малого». Шум и визг от железных скобок и ржавых винтов разбудили на другом конце города булочника, который, подняв свою алебарду, закричал спросонья что стало мочи: «Кто идет?» — но, увидев, что никто не шел, а слышалось только издали дребезжанье, поймал у себя на воротнике какого-то зверя и, подошед к фонарю, казнил его тут же у себя на ногте. После чего, отставивши алебарду, опять заснул по уставам своего рыцарства. Лошади то и дело падали на передние коленки, потому что не были подкованы, и притом, как видно, покойная городская мостовая была им мало знакома. Колымага, сделавши несколько поворотов из улицы в улицу, наконец поворотила в темный переулок мимо небольшой приходской церкви Николы на Недотычках и остановилась пред воротами дома протопопши. Из брички вылезла девка, с платком на голове, в телогрейке, и хватила обоими кулаками в ворота так сильно, хоть бы и мужчине (малый в куртке из пеструшки был уже потом стащен за ноги, ибо спал мертвецки). Собаки залаяли, и ворота, разинувшись наконец, проглотили, хотя с большим трудом, это неуклюжее дорожное произведение. Экипаж въехал в тесный двор, заваленный дровами, курятниками и всякими клетухами; из экипажа вылезла барыня: эта барыня была помещица, коллежская секретарша Коробочка. Старушка вскоре после отъезда нашего героя в такое пришла беспокойство насчет могущего произойти со стороны его обмана, что, не поспавши три ночи сряду, решилась ехать в город, несмотря на то что лошади не были подкованы, и там узнать наверно, почем ходят мертвые души и уж не промахнулась ли она, боже сохрани, продав их, может быть, втридешева. Какое произвело следствие это прибытие, читатель может узнать из одного разговора, который произошел между одними двумя дамами. Разговор сей… но пусть лучше сей разговор будет в следующей главе.

human_translations.translator_1: But while our hero was sitting in his hard armchair, troubled by sleeplessness and his thoughts, and vigorously cursing Nozdryov and all his relations, while before him glowed a tallow candle with a black cowl of soot on the wick, which threatened every minute to go out, while the blind, dark night, on the point of turning blue with the approaching dawn, looked in at the window, and in the distance cocks were crowing to one another, and in the slumbering town perhaps some poor fellow of unknown class and rank in a fustianda overcoat trudged along knowing nothing of aught but the highway, too well worn (alas!) by the vagabonds of Russia—at that very moment an event was taking place at the other end of the town that was destined to increase the unpleasantness of our hero’s position. To be precise, a strange equipage, for which it is puzzling to find a name, was creaking through the further streets and alleys of the town; it was not like a coach, nor a carriage, nor a chaise, but it was more like a full-cheeked rounded melon on wheels. The cheeks of this melon, that is the doors, which bore tracks of yellow paint, shut very badly owing to the rickety condition of the handles and locks, which were tied up with string. The melon was full of cotton cushions in the shape of pouches, rolling-pins and simple pillows, stuffed up with sacks of bread, fancy loaves, doughnuts and pasties, and bread rings made of boiled dough. Chicken pies and saltfish pies peeped out at the top. The footboard was occupied by an individual of the flunkey order, with an unshaven chin, slightly touched with grey, in a short jacket of bright-coloured homespun—the sort of individual known as a “fellow.” The clank and squeaking of the iron clamps and rusty screws woke a sentry at the other end of the town, who picking up his halberd shouted half awake at the top of his voice: “Who goes there?” but seeing that no one was passing, and only hearing a creaking in the distance, caught a beast of some sort on his collar, and, going up to a lamp-post, executed it on the spot with his nail, then laying aside his halberd, fell asleep again in accordance with the rules of his chivalry. The horses kept falling on their knees, for they had not been shod, and evidently the quiet cobbled streets of the town were unfamiliar to them. This grotesque equipage, after turning several times from one street into another, at last turned into a dark side-street next the little parish church of St. Nikolay, and stopped before the head priest’s gate. A girl clambered out of the vehicle, wearing a short warm jacket, with a kerchief on her head, and beat on the gate with both fists as though she were beating a man (the “fellow” in the bright-coloured homespun jacket was afterwards dragged down by his legs, for he was sleeping like the dead). Dogs began barking, the gates yawned, and at last, though with difficulty, swallowed up this uncouth monster of the road. The carriage drove into the narrow yard which was filled up with stacks of wood, poultry-houses and sheds; a lady alighted: this lady was no other than Madame Korobotchka. Soon after our hero’s departure, the old lady had been overcome by such anxiety as to the possibility of his deceiving her, that after lying awake for three nights in succession she made up her mind to drive into the town, regardless of the fact that the horses were not shod, hoping there to find out for certain what price dead souls were going for, and whether she had not—God forbid—made a terrible blunder by selling them at a third of their proper price. The effect produced by this incident may be understood by the reader from a conversation which took place between two ladies. This conversation—but this conversation had better be kept for the following chapter.
human_translations.translator_2: In short, Nozdrev’s whole lineage was passed in review; and many of its members in the ascending line fared badly in the process. Meanwhile, at the other end of the town there was in progress an event which was destined to augment still further the unpleasantness of our hero’s position. That is to say, through the outlying streets and alleys of the town there was clattering a vehicle to which it would be difficult precisely to assign a name, seeing that, though it was of a species peculiar to itself, it most nearly resembled a large, rickety water melon on wheels. Eventually this monstrosity drew up at the gates of a house where the archpriest of one of the churches resided, and from its doors there leapt a damsel clad in a jerkin and wearing a scarf over her head. For a while she thumped the gates so vigorously as to set all the dogs barking; then the gates stiffly opened, and admitted this unwieldy phenomenon of the road. Lastly, the barinia herself alighted, and stood revealed as Madame Korobotchka, widow of a Collegiate Secretary! The reason of her sudden arrival was that she had felt so uneasy about the possible outcome of Chichikov’s whim, that during the three nights following his departure she had been unable to sleep a wink; whereafter, in spite of the fact that her horses were not shod, she had set off for the town, in order to learn at first hand how the dead souls were faring, and whether (which might God forfend!) she had not sold them at something like a third of their true value. The consequences of her venture the reader will learn from a conversation between two ladies. We will reserve it for the ensuing chapter.

What consequences this arrival produced, the reader may learn from a certain conversation that took place between a certain two ladies. human_translations.translator_4: But while Chichikov was sitting in his uneasy chair, troubled by his thoughts and sleeplessness, heartily reviling Nozdrev and all his kith and kin, and before him warmly glowed a tallow candle, the wick of which had long since become covered with candle snuff as if with a black cowl and was threatening to go out at any moment, and sightless, black night was peering in at the windows, just about to turn bluish because of the approaching dawn, and roosters, afar off, were exchanging their clarion calls, and throughout the town, all sunk in slumber, there may not have been a soul out on the streets save for some frieze overcoat tipsily weaving along somewhere, some poor wretch, his class and rank unknown, and himself knowing only (alas!) the path, all too deeply beaten and much trodden by the unruly, loose, hard-drinking Russian folk—at this time, in another quarter of the town, an event was taking place which was about to augment the unpleasantness of our hero’s position. To be precise, through the remote streets and by-lanes of the town a quite odd vehicle, which made one wonder what name one could give it, was jarringly lumbering along. It resembled neither a tarantass, nor a calash, nor a light covered carriage, but rather a round-cheeked, bulging watermelon placed on wheels. The cheeks of this watermelon—i.e., its small doors— which still bore traces of yellow paint, closed but poorly, owing to the sad state of the handles and catches, which were haphazardly tied together with bits of rope. The watermelon was filled to bursting with calico pillows shaped like tobacco pouches, like bolsters, or simply like pillows; it was stuffed with bags of bread loaves (plain and braided), egg buns, dumplings, and pretzels of biscuit dough. There was even a chicken pie and another of salted beef, both peeping coyly out of one of the bags. The footboard behind was occupied by a person of flunky extraction, in a short jacket of homespun striped ticking, his chin unshaven and his head slightly grizzled—a person usually described as a “lad.” The noise and whining from the iron clamps and rusty bolts awakened, at the other end of the town, a sentry in his box, who, picking up his halberd, set up a shout with all his might, though still half asleep: “Who goes there?” But, perceiving that no one was going there and that there was only a clatter of wheels in the distance, he contented himself with catching some beastie or other on his coat collar and, walking up to a street lamp, executing it summarily on his thumbnail, after which, putting his halberd away in a corner, he again fell asleep, according to all the canons of his order of knighthood. The horses were forever stumbling to their foreknees, since they were not shod and, in addition to that, had but little acquaintance with the restful paved road of the town. This antediluvian shandrydan, having made several turns from one street to another, finally turned into a dark by-lane near the small parish church of Nikola-Out-in-the-Sticks and stopped before the house of the Archpriests wife. But continuing the previous scene, where he sat in his hard chair, tormented by thoughts and insomnia, plied with zealously Nosdrev and all his family, and in front of him a greasy candle flickered, which had long since been shrouded in a dark cap of soot, threatening to go out every minute, and stared at him through the windows with a blind, dark night, ready to pale from the approaching dawn, and the distant distant roosters whistled, and in a completely asleep city, maybe somewhere a cotton jacket was being sewn by a wretched person of an unknown class and dignity, who knew only a path excessively worn down by the Russian mob - in that time, on the other end of the city, an event occurred, which prepared to increase the unpleasantness of our hero's situation. 

It was precisely in the remote streets and alleys of the city that a very strange carriage rattled, causing perplexity as to its name. It was not like a cart, nor a carriage, nor a coach, but rather resembled a thick-skinned, convex gourd, placed on wheels. The cheeks of this gourd, i.e., the doors, with signs of yellow paint, closed very poorly due to the poor state of the handles and locks, somewhat tied with ropes. The gourd was filled with patchwork pillows in the shape of tobacco pouches, rolls and simply pillows, stuffed with bags of bread, kalach, koulouri, kutiyah, and zeppole doughnuts. The pastries of the apple strudel and the pirozhok were even peeking out. The gentleman of the footman's origin, with a face of nobility, in a fur-lined coat, with a bearded face, covered with a slight balding, had his face turned to the eyebrows, and a questioning look on his face. A sound and scream from the iron brackets and rusty bolts awoke another end of the city, a baker, who, grasping his alabaster, shouted drowsily, "Who's coming?" - but, seeing that no one was coming, and only heard a distant rattling, caught a beast on his own neck and, approaching the lantern, executed him there on his own toe. 

After which, putting away the alabaster, he fell asleep again according to the principles of his chivalry. The horses often fell on their front knees, because they were not horseshoeed, and, as it was visible, were not familiar with the city's cobblestone pavement. The kalymag, making several turns from one street to another, finally turned into a dark alley near a small church of Nicholas on Nedozyotchki and stopped in front of the protopop's house gates. A girl got out of the carriage, with a headscarf on her head, in a woolen coat, and she slapped both fists into the gates so hard that, even a man (the small gentleman in a fur-lined coat was already then dragged by his legs, because he was sleeping dead asleep). The dogs barked, and the gates, finally yawning, swallowed up this clumsy road vehicle, although with great difficulty. 

The carriage drove into a narrow courtyard, littered with logs, chickens, and various cage-like things; a baroness got out of the carriage: this baroness was the mistress, a collegiate secretary, Korobochka. 

The old lady, soon after our hero left, came into such a worry about the possibility of deception on his part that, not having slept for three nights in a row, she decided to go to the city, despite the fact that the horses were not horseshoeed, and there, perhaps, find out how the dead souls are doing and whether she had not sold them, God preserve her, for a trifle. What a consequence this arrival had, the reader can find out from one conversation between two ladies. The conversation is... but let this conversation be in the next chapter.
source_text: Но в продолжение того, как он сидел в жестких своих креслах, тревожимый мыслями и бессонницей, угощая усердно Ноздрева и всю родню его, и перед ним теплилась сальная свечка, которой светильня давно уже накрылась нагоревшею черною шапкою, ежеминутно грозя погаснуть, и глядела ему в окна слепая, темная ночь, готовая посинеть от приближавшегося рассвета, и пересвистывались вдали отдаленные петухи, и в совершенно заснувшем городе, может быть, плелась где-нибудь фризовая шинель, горемыка неизвестно какого класса и чина, знающая одну только (увы!) слишком протертую русским забубенным народом дорогу, — в это время на другом конце города происходило событие, которое готовилось увеличить неприятность положения нашего героя. Именно, в отдаленных улицах и закоулках города дребезжал весьма странный экипаж, наводивший недоумение насчет своего названия. Он не был похож ни на тарантас, ни на коляску, ни на бричку, а был скорее похож на толстощекий выпуклый арбуз, поставленный на колеса. Щеки этого арбуза, то есть дверцы, носившие следы желтой краски, затворялись очень плохо по причине плохого состояния ручек и замков, кое-как связанных веревками. Арбуз был наполнен ситцевыми подушками в виде кисетов, валиков и просто подушек, напичкан мешками с хлебами, калачами, кокурками, скородумками и кренделями из заварного теста. Пирог-курник и пирог-рассольник выглядывали даже наверх. Запятки были заняты лицом лакейского происхожденья, в куртке из домашней пеструшки, с небритой бородою, подернутою легкой проседью, — лицо, известное под именем «малого». Шум и визг от железных скобок и ржавых винтов разбудили на другом конце города булочника, который, подняв свою алебарду, закричал спросонья что стало мочи: «Кто идет?» — но, увидев, что никто не шел, а слышалось только издали дребезжанье, поймал у себя на воротнике какого-то зверя и, подошед к фонарю, казнил его тут же у себя на ногте. После чего, отставивши алебарду, опять заснул по уставам своего рыцарства. Лошади то и дело падали на передние коленки, потому что не были подкованы, и притом, как видно, покойная городская мостовая была им мало знакома. Колымага, сделавши несколько поворотов из улицы в улицу, наконец поворотила в темный переулок мимо небольшой приходской церкви Николы на Недотычках и остановилась пред воротами дома протопопши. Из брички вылезла девка, с платком на голове, в телогрейке, и хватила обоими кулаками в ворота так сильно, хоть бы и мужчине (малый в куртке из пеструшки был уже потом стащен за ноги, ибо спал мертвецки). Собаки залаяли, и ворота, разинувшись наконец, проглотили, хотя с большим трудом, это неуклюжее дорожное произведение. Экипаж въехал в тесный двор, заваленный дровами, курятниками и всякими клетухами; из экипажа вылезла барыня: эта барыня была помещица, коллежская секретарша Коробочка. Старушка вскоре после отъезда нашего героя в такое пришла беспокойство насчет могущего произойти со стороны его обмана, что, не поспавши три ночи сряду, решилась ехать в город, несмотря на то что лошади не были подкованы, и там узнать наверно, почем ходят мертвые души и уж не промахнулась ли она, боже сохрани, продав их, может быть, втридешева. Какое произвело следствие это прибытие, читатель может узнать из одного разговора, который произошел между одними двумя дамами. Разговор сей… но пусть лучше сей разговор будет в следующей главе.
gt_translation: But as he sat in his hard armchair, troubled by thoughts and insomnia, diligently treating Nozdryov and all his relatives, a tallow candle flickered in front of him, with which the lamp had long been covered with a burning black hat, every minute threatening to go out, and looked into his blind, dark night, ready to turn blue from the approaching dawn, and distant roosters whistled in the distance, and in the completely asleep city, perhaps, somewhere a frieze overcoat was woven somewhere, a miserable man of unknown class and rank, who knows only one (alas!) too worn the road to the Russian people, beaten down by the people, - at that time, at the other end of the city, an event was taking place that was preparing to increase the unpleasantness of the position of our hero. Indeed, in the remote streets and back streets of the city, a very strange carriage rattled, suggesting bewilderment about its name. It did not look like a carriage, or a carriage, or a britzka, but rather looked like a fat-cheeked, convex watermelon set on wheels. The cheeks of this watermelon, that is, the doors, which bore traces of yellow paint, closed very poorly due to the poor condition of the handles and locks, somehow tied with ropes. A noise and a screech from iron brackets and rusty screws woke up a baker at the other end of the city, who, raising his halberd, yelled in his waking breath: "Who's coming?" - but, seeing that no one was walking, and only a rattling was heard from afar, he caught some animal on his collar and, going up to the lantern, executed him right there on his fingernail. human_translations.translator_1: But while our hero was sitting in his hard armchair, troubled by sleeplessness and his thoughts, and vigorously cursing Nozdryov and all his relations, while before him glowed a tallow candle with a black cowl of soot on the wick, which threatened every minute to go out, while the blind, dark night, on the point of turning blue with the approaching dawn, looked in at the window, and in the distance cocks were crowing to one another, and in the slumbering town perhaps some poor fellow of unknown class and rank in a fustianda overcoat trudged along knowing nothing of aught but the highway, too well worn (alas!) by the vagabonds of Russia—at that very moment an event was taking place at the other end of the town that was destined to increase the unpleasantness of our hero’s position. To be precise, a strange equipage, for which it is puzzling to find a name, was creaking through the further streets and alleys of the town; it was not like a coach, nor a carriage, nor a chaise, but it was more like a full-cheeked rounded melon on wheels. The cheeks of this melon, that is the doors, which bore tracks of yellow paint, shut very badly owing to the rickety condition of the handles and locks, which were tied up with string. The melon was full of cotton cushions in the shape of pouches, rolling-pins and simple pillows, stuffed up with sacks of bread, fancy loaves, doughnuts and pasties, and bread rings made of boiled dough. Chicken pies and saltfish pies peeped out at the top. The footboard was occupied by an individual of the flunkey order, with an unshaven chin, slightly touched with grey, in a short jacket of bright-coloured homespun—the sort of individual known as a “fellow.” The clank and squeaking of the iron clamps and rusty screws woke a sentry at the other end of the town, who picking up his halberd shouted half awake at the top of his voice: “Who goes there?” but seeing that no one was passing, and only hearing a creaking in the distance, caught a beast of some sort on his collar, and, going up to a lamp-post, executed it on the spot with his nail, then laying aside his halberd, fell asleep again in accordance with the rules of his chivalry. The horses kept falling on their knees, for they had not been shod, and evidently the quiet cobbled streets of the town were unfamiliar to them. This grotesque equipage, after turning several times from one street into another, at last turned into a dark side-street next the little parish church of St. Nikolay, and stopped before the head priest’s gate. A girl clambered out of the vehicle, wearing a short warm jacket, with a kerchief on her head, and beat on the gate with both fists as though she were beating a man (the “fellow” in the bright-coloured homespun jacket was afterwards dragged down by his legs, for he was sleeping like the dead). Dogs began barking, the gates yawned, and at last, though with difficulty, swallowed up this uncouth monster of the road. The carriage drove into the narrow yard which was filled up with stacks of wood, poultry-houses and sheds; a lady alighted: this lady was no other than Madame Korobotchka. Soon after our hero’s departure, the old lady had been overcome by such anxiety as to the possibility of his deceiving her, that after lying awake for three nights in succession she made up her mind to drive into the town, regardless of the fact that the horses were not shod, hoping there to find out for certain what price dead souls were going for, and whether she had not—God forbid—made a terrible blunder by selling them at a third of their proper price. The effect produced by this incident may be understood by the reader from a conversation which took place between two ladies. This conversation—but this conversation had better be kept for the following chapter.
human_translations.translator_2: In short, Nozdrev’s whole lineage was passed in review; and many of its members in the ascending line fared badly in the process. Meanwhile, at the other end of the town there was in progress an event which was destined to augment still further the unpleasantness of our hero’s position. That is to say, through the outlying streets and alleys of the town there was clattering a vehicle to which it would be difficult precisely to assign a name, seeing that, though it was of a species peculiar to itself, it most nearly resembled a large, rickety water melon on wheels. Eventually this monstrosity drew up at the gates of a house where the archpriest of one of the churches resided, and from its doors there leapt a damsel clad in a jerkin and wearing a scarf over her head. For a while she thumped the gates so vigorously as to set all the dogs barking; then the gates stiffly opened, and admitted this unwieldy phenomenon of the road. Lastly, the barinia herself alighted, and stood revealed as Madame Korobotchka, widow of a Collegiate Secretary! The reason of her sudden arrival was that she had felt so uneasy about the possible outcome of Chichikov’s whim, that during the three nights following his departure she had been unable to sleep a wink; whereafter, in spite of the fact that her horses were not shod, she had set off for the town, in order to learn at first hand how the dead souls were faring, and whether (which might God forfend!) she had not sold them at something like a third of their true value. The consequences of her venture the reader will learn from a conversation between two ladies. We will reserve it for the ensuing chapter.
human_translations.translator_3: But all the while he was sitting in his hard armchair, troubled by thoughts and sleeplessness, zealously giving what for to Nozdryov and all his kin, and the tallow candle glimmered before him, its wick long covered by a black cap of snuff, threatening to go out at any moment, and blind, dark night looked in his window, ready to turn blue with approaching dawn, and somewhere far away far-off roosters whistled to each other, and in a completely sleeping town, perhaps, a frieze greatcoat plodded along somewhere, a wretch of unknown class and rank, who knows (alas!) one path only, all too well beaten by the devil-may-care Russian people—during this time, at the other end of town, an event was taking place which was about to increase the unpleasantness of our hero’s situation. Namely, through the remote streets and alleys of the town there came clattering a rather strange vehicle, causing bewilderment with regard to its name. It resembled neither a tarantass, nor a barouche, nor a britzka, but more closely resembled a round, fat-cheeked watermelon on wheels. The cheeks of this watermelon—the doors, that is—bearing traces of yellow paint, closed very poorly on account of the poor condition of the handles and latches, which were tied anyhow with string. human_translations.translator_4: But while Chichikov was sitting in his uneasy chair, troubled by his thoughts and sleeplessness, heartily reviling Nozdrev and all his kith and kin, and before him warmly glowed a tallow candle, the wick of which had long since become covered with candle snuff as if with a black cowl and was threatening to go out at any moment, and sightless, black night was peering in at the windows, just about to turn bluish because of the approaching dawn, and roosters, afar off, were exchanging their clarion calls, and throughout the town, all sunk in slumber, there may not have been a soul out on the streets save for some frieze overcoat tipsily weaving along somewhere, some poor wretch, his class and rank unknown, and himself knowing only (alas!) the path, all too deeply beaten and much trodden by the unruly, loose, hard-drinking Russian folk—at this time, in another quarter of the town, an event was taking place which was about to augment the unpleasantness of our hero’s position. To be precise, through the remote streets and by-lanes of the town a quite odd vehicle, which made one wonder what name one could give it, was jarringly lumbering along. It resembled neither a tarantass, nor a calash, nor a light covered carriage, but rather a round-cheeked, bulging watermelon placed on wheels. The cheeks of this watermelon—i.e., its small doors— which still bore traces of yellow paint, closed but poorly, owing to the sad state of the handles and catches, which were haphazardly tied together with bits of rope. The watermelon was filled to bursting with calico pillows shaped like tobacco pouches, like bolsters, or simply like pillows; it was stuffed with bags of bread loaves (plain and braided), egg buns, dumplings, and pretzels of biscuit dough. There was even a chicken pie and another of salted beef, both peeping coyly out of one of the bags. The footboard behind was occupied by a person of flunky extraction, in a short jacket of homespun striped ticking, his chin unshaven and his head slightly grizzled—a person usually described as a “lad.” The noise and whining from the iron clamps and rusty bolts awakened, at the other end of the town, a sentry in his box, who, picking up his halberd, set up a shout with all his might, though still half asleep: “Who goes there?” But, perceiving that no one was going there and that there was only a clatter of wheels in the distance, he contented himself with catching some beastie or other on his coat collar and, walking up to a street lamp, executing it summarily on his thumbnail, after which, putting his halberd away in a corner, he again fell asleep, according to all the canons of his order of knighthood. The horses were forever stumbling to their foreknees, since they were not shod and, in addition to that, had but little acquaintance with the restful paved road of the town. This antediluvian shandrydan, having made several turns from one street to another, finally turned into a dark by-lane near the small parish church of Nikola-Out-in-the-Sticks and stopped before the house of the Archpriests wife. A wench with a kerchief on her head and dressed in a warm, sleeveless jacket, crawled out of the vehicle and began pounding with her fists on the gate as hard as any man could have done (the lad in the short jacket of striped ticking was only later on dragged off his perch by his feet, inasmuch as he was sleeping the sleep of the dead). Dogs began barking, and the gates, gaping open at last, swallowed, though with difficulty, this cumbersome conveyance. It drove into a crowded yard, cluttered with firewood, henhouses, and all sorts of flimsy coops and hutches; a gentlewoman climbed out of the vehicle; this gentlewoman being none other than Korobochka the landowner, widow of a collegiate secretary. Soon after our hero’s departure the little crone had been overcome by such uneasiness about a possible raw deal on his part that, after losing sleep for three nights in a row, she had decided to go into town—despite the fact that her horses were not shod—and there learn for sure what dead souls were fetching and whether she hadn’t— God forbid!—missed a trick in selling them for what may have been next to nothing. What effect this arrival brought about the reader may learn from a certain conversation which took place between a certain two ladies. This conversation .. . but better let this conversation come in the next chapter.
